subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-CANADIAN POSITION RESPECTING PENDING RESOLUTIONS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-CANADIAN POSITION RESPECTING PENDING RESOLUTIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs to place before the house the position of the Canadian government in respect of the several resolutions now before the United Nations general assembly. In particular I would ask him to clarify the position outlined in a speech by Ambassador Ignatieff on the Pakistan resolution calling for the nullification of Israel's annexation of the old city of Jerusalem. Is that interpretation the stand of the Canadian government? Is this a correct interpretation, although contrary to suggestions made by the Prime Minister, according to various representatives of the Jewish faith? Has the government decided to vote in favour of a resolution to nullify the action taken by Israel in asserting municipal government to cover the entire city?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of Stale for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-CANADIAN POSITION RESPECTING PENDING RESOLUTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the difficulties in answering such a question on orders of the day is that it is not possible to go into all aspects of the situation. There are a number of resolutions before the general assembly at the present time. This particular resolution has not been dealt with and may not be voted on today, according to the most recent information. There are discussions presently taking place in connection with this resolution, and until these discussions have been completed I do not believe it would be responsible to go beyond what I have said.
However, with regard to another resolution, that standing in the name of the Latin American countries, there is a provision in the final operative paragraph that note should be taken of resolutions passed by the 1949 assembly of the United Nations calling for the establishment of an international regime in Jerusalem. This resolution reaffirms earlier recommendations for an international regime,
but proposes that consideration of this question should not be taken until the next general assembly.
We had not voted for the 1949 resolutions but we were in favour of international supervision and protection of access to the holy places of the three great religions. I do not believe at this time I could go beyond that.
The resolution to which my hon. friend referred is in the name of Pakistan. It calls for an expression of opinion from the United Nations assembly asking the government of Israel not to proceed with the annexation of Jerusalem. It does not do so in exactly those terms, but that is the implication of the resolution. That resolution is now being discussed in private consultations.
If Canada were to take the position suggested by my right hon. friend it might be inconsistent with the position we took in our statement at the general assembly, when we said that there should be no precipitate action taken, no freezing of any negotiating positions, and that there should of course be, as Israel will provide, access to the holy places. But let there be no doubt about this; with regard to the Latin American resolution Canada will not agree to the withdrawal of Israeli forces unless it is related to the termination of belligerency, and also to the recognition of the basic issues involved. This was covered in the six points made by the Prime Minister when he spoke here six weeks ago.

subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-CANADIAN POSITION RESPECTING PENDING RESOLUTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with great respect to the minister I would not consider that statement as much of a clarification. I will come back to the question. On the Pakistan resolution, of which the minister was kind enough to give the purport, is it a fact that Mr. Ignatieff indicated in the assembly that Canada would support that resolution? That is the first question. The second question is this. The hon. gentleman said I had suggested certain action by Canada. That is not so. I asked a question concerning what Canada's stand is going to be. I am trying as hard as I can to understand what it is. That is the reason I asked the simple question, how does Canada intend to vote on the Pakistan resolution?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs whether Canada has taken any steps to recommend the appointment of an international or United Nations commissioner for the city of Jerusalem or whether she has taken any initiative toward recommending a mediator between Israel and the Arab nations representing the United Nations or any other international body.

speechtext: Before the security council there is a resolution standing in the name of Canada, which has not yet been disposed of. It provides for the appointment of a representative of the Secretary General to try to bring about negotiation between the parties. subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-CANADIAN POSITION RESPECTING PENDING RESOLUTIONS
speechtext: I should like to go back to my supplementary question, asking whether Canada has taken any initiative toward recommending the establishment of a commissioner or mediator to act in respect of the conflicting parties in the Middle East crisis. He did not answer that question.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I thought I said clearly that in the resolution we have put before the security council there is provision for that very suggestion. maintopic: VIET NAM-CONSIDERATION OF PROPOSALS ADVANCED BY J. K. GALBRAITH
speechtext: In reply to the particular question asked by my right hon. friend, let me say I am sure he will realize that vital matters of foreign policy are not settled in the way my right hon. friend is suggesting. He should not be overly moved by any political convention that is being held anywhere in Canada in regard to matters that are as vital as this. Mr. Speaker, may I deal with the matter my right hon. friend has introduced. I do not recall the right hon. gentleman's exact words but I would like to make it clear that in whatever arrangements were made for Her Majesty's visit to Expo yesterday the government was of course moved by considerations which must be in

the mind of any Canadian government, and which I am sure would have been in the mind of my right hon. friend had he been sitting on this side as head of the government.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the other day when we had a brief discussion on the first item of the minister's estimates I did not have the opportunity, because time ran out, to make a few remarks on the full report of the committee, limiting myself to that part of the report that deals with the western parks. The
July 4, 1967

minister knows well from the past my interest in this particular matter. I must say that I think the committee members from the government side in particular received their first exposure to the parks on their trip there last December, some of them never having seen them before. I think that this fact is shown up in the type of report that has been prepared and presented. Government members were distinctly under the whip in the matter of following a hard government line on the national parks.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
I do not think there was any great difference in point of view among members of the committee as to the ultimate purpose of the parks, although there may have been some difference of opinion as to how that purpose would be best achieved. Very definitely, though, we on this side of the house, who have the greatest contact with the parks, did express a fundamental difference of opinion with regard to certain existing factors. The minister can say what he likes about the relationship between the officials of his department and the citizens of the townsites of Jasper and Banff in particular. He can say that the relationship is good, but this is not the case. What has happened is the result of the department taking a hard and uncompromising line with regard to both commercial and residential leases, and there has been a lamentable breakdown in the relationship between the administration and the citizens.
There is one thing the higher officials of the parks branch must remember. They cannot, by a stroke of an administrative pen, eliminate those townsites. They are historical facts. They do exist. Moreover, their existence creates special problems which do not arise in any of the parks outside the province of Alberta. When the decision was taken years ago to route the trans-Canada highway through Banff national park, certain inevitable consequences were entailed. There is no question that hundreds of thousands of tourists who visit the parks or pass through them on their way west expect to stay in the parks. I do not suppose anyone quarrels with that. How are these people to be treated?
I am the last to say that Banff or Jasper should be turned into a Coney Island type of development. On the other hand, there is a change in the needs and desires of the travelling public. They are no longer prepared to accept substandard accommodation. They will not be directed to the nth degree with regard to what they should or should not do while on holiday. We have invited these people. Look
Supply-Indian Affairs at the advertisements put out by the government travel bureau. We have spent scores of thousands of dollars inviting tourists to come to our national parks. What are they to do when they arrive? Take only a flying trip? Not at all. They must be catered to if our tourist program is to be meaningful.
Pressure on the available facilities during the last few years has been scandalous during the peak season. Within a short time there will be a further increase in visitors to Jasper upon the completion of the Yellowhead route. I venture to say that by the fall of 1968 or perhaps by mid-1969 this essential link will have been established west of Jasper, bringing on a veritable flood of travellers. The only thing that will discourage them and give the parks a black eye will be lack of accommodation.
We know there has been hesitation, procrastination and uncertainty with regard to the development of accommodation in Jasper in anticipation of these visitors. It is no use saying that in 1969 or 1970, when we see the tourists coming through, we will build the essential facilities for them. Yet the present policy with regard to commercial leases discourages any meaningful development within the appropriate zoning of Jasper.
I wish to be clearly understood that I support the idea of zoning within the parks of Banff and Jasper. There should be service sections within the towns and then, because there is a complete monopoly by the national parks authorities of the mountain sites accessible by roads to the people of Alberta, there should also be amusement areas-skiing areas -in both places so as to use the facilities available to the full in winter.
We know that the present limited facilities are hard pressed even in winter. People who wish to ski at Jasper and Banff find it hard to obtain accommodation. Whenever I go out to Edmonton in winter I hear continual complaints from friends and acquaintances who love to ski that they find it difficult to get accommodation. Those who are more fortunate and more insistent go south to the state of Montana. This, I think, is the epitomy of idiocy, to insist that Canadians from Edmonton and Calgary should travel to the United States to enjoy week end skiing simply because they cannot get accommodation at Jasper and Banff. We have the facilities if we could only decide how to use them.
It is all very well for people to say there are no provincial parks in the mountains. One has only to look at the mountains from the

July 4, 1967
Supply-Indian Affairs area north of Jasper down to the United States border to see how little is accessible in relationship to roads and accommodation outside the boundaries of the parks. Scores of millions of dollars have been spent building the roads and a great deal of money has been invested in facilities. How foolish it is, then, to say that these assets should not be used in wintertime. If people want to engage in winter sports they must find another area.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
As yet the province of Alberta has dedicated more than enough land to be given over to national parks use. Its proportion is multifold that of all the rest of Canada, and in that you must take into account what is taken by the crown of Canada for various facilities, One is not going to say, "You are not going to have your winter sports at Elk Island," and I am going to speak about that park later, or "You are going to have your winter sports at Wood Buffalo national park."

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: You could.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
The minister, who has air travel facilities at his beck and call, can go up there if he wants, but it is hundreds of miles from populated centres and its limited facilities would be available only to people who have a lot of money. Young people, students and so forth, have as much right to enjoy skiing as anybody else. Therefore I believe an adequate zoning system should be established in the parks at the earliest possible date. There is no use appointing another commission or committee which will bring in another report two years hence. The time to do it is now.
With regard to our national parks there have been recommendations upon recommendations upon recommendations, but the end result has been the same. There has been some limited improvement. However, the demand made upon Banff, for example, far exceeds the facilities that have been provided.
Policy decisions have been arbitrary. Under the planning and zoning restrictions at Banff certain proposals have been turned down out of hand; yet changes have been authorized that were contrary to the zoning regulations. These will form the subject of an interesting study one of these days.
I now turn to the question of leases. I find the minister's attitude with regard to the controversial perpetual leases absolutely incomprehensible. His officials have advised him, and I am not questioning their motives, that there was never authority for the granting of

perpetual leases both prior and subsequent to 1932. The minister first asserted that there was a question about ministerial authority to grant perpetual leases after 1932. That is a debatable legal point. Now he says that there was no authority to do so prior to 1932.
The minister, who is trustee for the crown for the interests of Canadians, not a trustee on behalf of himself or any particular administration, refuses to disclose the memorandum of advice or the reasons for calling into question the jurisdiction to issue such leases. In refusing I think he has taken an entirely wrong position. He has told us, "If the holders of perpetual leases are not satisfied with their position they can go to court." His attitude is similar to that of one late crowned head who once said, "If they can't have bread, let them eat cake."
In fairness to his responsibility to his officials and to the scores, likely hundreds, of holders of perpetual leases, the minister should refer the question of the validity of the leases to the courts. He should not ask a young teacher and his wife in Banff, or some person with limited means, to challenge the government in the courts. Who would pay the costs in such an instance? No doubt there would be solicitor and client costs which would be the responsibility of the individual. It would be very simple for the minister to have a stated case referred to the Exchequer Court or the Supreme Court, most likely the Exchequer Court in the first instance, with permission for intervention on behalf of the holders of perpetual leases. I believe he should take this course immediately instead of trying to wear down and chisel away the individual lease holders who are finding themselves being cornered more and more, without any possible alternative.
In some of the cases about which I have heard, almost administrative blackmail is being utilized to pressure the holders of leases to agree to exchange their leases for limited term leases, and not all of the same term. This is quite unacceptable. This not litigation between two individuals. This is an honest difference of opinion between the law officers of the crown and hundreds of citizens who have as much entitlement to their rights as do any of us in this chamber or in the administration to ours.
In the past there was never any question that they were acquiring defeasible leases of uncertain title. I urge upon the minister that in all justice the crown should settle this matter by causing a stated case to be referred
July 4, 1967

to the superior courts. It is not fair for the minister to tell leaseholders when they seek to renew their leases on the terms contained in them, terms authorized by the minister's predecessors, that unless they agree to new conditions not negotiated but imposed by the minister and his officials they will be deemed to be overholding tenants subject to all the consequences that befall overholding tenants.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
In so far as commercial leases are concerned I should like to draw to the attention of the minister an editorial which appeared in the Edmonton Journal of May 23. I am sure his officials know about it, if he does not. It reads:
This newspaper has said repeatedly that Mr. Arthur Laing's national parks policy is not a valid policy so far as it governs commercial leases. Here's a case in point:
An Edmonton group planned a 77-unit motel at Jasper, assembled $450,000 in cash, arranged $550,000 in mortage funds, obtained the parks department's approval of a site in Jasper town-then cancelled its plans. The reason given: no compensation when the lease expires. The money is still available; so is the building site. But until there is compensation for cancelled commercial leases, say the investors, they won't go into Jasper.
It is conceded that this might be a pressure play, a mandate to call on investment for badly needed accommodation if the terms are right. But is that a valid argument for cancelling the whole thing? Is it not a little more in the interest of the general public to have a parks policy which at one and the same time protects the park from undesirable commercial development-no one denies that the minister has all sorts of restrictions on that score-and encourages desirable development? One of the most desirable, indeed the most urgent, developments required now at Jasper is more decent accommodation. The newspaper editorial continues:
One long time Jasper hotel operator says he could fill another 1.000 rooms all summer; but no major hotel or motel has been built in Jasper since Mr. Laing's no-compensation policy was announced. Of four groups officially announced as having plans to build in Jasper, we are informed, all four have changed their minds.
We don't favour so-called "perpetual leases" and doubt that responsible investors do. Leases should be cancelled when operators fail on performance standards. Leases should have to be renewed regularly. Some leases should be cancelled when the public interest requires a different use of a site. But in such cases, and varying with the cause of cancellation, there ought to be reasonable compensation-by arbitration, if necessary.
I could go into detail with regard to the yeas and nays of the leasehold policy, an abridged version of which I have. After all,
Supply-Indian Affairs who on earth would want to invest hundreds of thousands of dollars and perhaps over a million dollars over a period of years in a commercial proposition when at the end of that term the title is gone and everything

buildings, maintenance and some modernization over a 21-year period

is yielded up to the crown? Who on earth is going to invest even one thin dime during the last five-year period, or perhaps during a period of eight or ten years, in a commercial leasehold property, if at the end of the road there is to be one big fat zero in compensation?
Even now we see the iniquities of the policies of the present minister. Because of the increased demand a store proprietor must modernize and expand his premises. He holds a perpetual lease and has had it for a long, time. But because he wants to make improvements he is told that if he is to get his permit he must yield his perpetual lease and take a limited term lease on which at the end there will be no compensation. Is there no justice between the crown and the individual? What is his alternative? Is it to let his premises run down to rack and ruin so that he loses his capital? Perhaps his life's work is tied up in the good will and continuity of that business. Yet because of administrative reasons, because somebody wants to get hold of something and squeeze it hard, then, unless it is to be contained within a nice neat framework of rules and regulations administered from far away, that man's effort is to be sacrificed. I cite that as an example of many cases and of the general principle.
It is indeed unfortunate that the government majority on the committee had limited exposure to the problem. True, they saw and heard a number of people, some of whom were very dramatic. I hope some of them were ashamed of some of the administrative boondoggling that has gone on with regard to the treatment of these people. I am not limiting that in time either.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: What is boondoggling?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: The minister can look it up.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
In any event these people have been mishandled. I realize that efforts are being made to bring about improvements, and this is all to the good, but for the life of me I cannot see why these people who have certain rights should be denied them. If it is decided that there shall be no more perpetual leases granted, then this is fine in respect of

July 4, 1967
Supply-Indian Affairs new leases or for the development of further practices. But there are such things as acquired rights. If we were to tell the minister that because of a change in administrative policy his home in Vancouver would be subject to different terms, in respect of his title and right of ownership, than those under which he holds his property now, then I say the hullabaloo would be heard from one end of the country to the other.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I ask for the indulgence of the committee to allow me one more minute to conclude my remarks? I think I have said enough on this last point.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
I apologize to hon. members for requiring this extra time, but there is one further point I should like to draw to the minister's attention. With the development of the Yellowhead Pass route there will be a considerable acceleration of travel through our national parks, not only Jasper national park but Elk Island park. I know that my colleague, the hon. member for Vegreville, would like to speak about this matter if he were here.
Highway 16 east in Alberta bisects Elk Island park which over the years has unfortunately been one of the Cinderellas of our parks system. This park has great potential and although this highway has never been qualified as a second trans-Canada route, as suggested by members from the western provinces, it is being developed. This highway will give greater access to the national parks which lie along it including Jasper, Elk Island, and even Prince Albert national park which is some distance north. Anyone travelling this route could easily turn up toward Prince Albert national park. It would also give access to Riding Mountain national park in Manitoba. These parks are all either along the highway or within reasonable access.
My suggestion is that an immediate study be make, if it has not been already made, of methods to upgrade public reception facilities. I am not suggesting that we should allow the establishment of residential townsites in these parks such as Elk Island, but public

reception services must be upgraded. I am sure this would pay dividends in the form of increased patronage and enjoyment by the public. My suggestion is that we begin a study immediately and within the next two or three years make the improvements. We should not wait for ten years to do so because a lot of traffic will be channeled through these areas and Canadians will then find that their national parks are truly accessible. In order to enjoy these parks one should not have to be a dedicated wildlife conservationist such as some of those we heard from in Banff and Jasper. Their philosophy seemed to be that we should build a ten-foot fence around our parks, lock the gates and throw away the keys. They felt it would be abusive to allow any but simple activities such as bird watching, nature study or peaceful hiking.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: The attendance at our parks has been increasing by 15 per cent compounded per year for years.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: I do not feel that the one extreme should be the standard, nor do I feel that we should have the so-called Coney Island level of development. That would not be desirable nor acceptable.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few remarks at this stage of our deliberations in respect of the educational program in Canada's north. In the last decade we have observed a fairly impressive increase in the number of young people attending school in the north. We know that 13 or 14 years ago approximately 30 per cent of our young northern Indians, Eskimos and Metis were attending school along with whites. In 1954 and 1955 the federal government recognized its responsibility in respect of the development of educational facilities throughout Canada's north and we have observed the construction of schools in virtually all communities there. As a result approximately 90 to 95 per cent of the young people of school age are attending school. Administrations of the past deserve a great deal of credit for what has taken place in this regard. I think we have now reached the stage when our aims and objectives in respect of education in the north must be redefined.
Having attended the graduation exercises at two of our northern schools in recent weeks I could not help but be impressed by the dedication of these young students. The system developed over the past few years has been directed not only to book learning as part of education but to a broadening of the
July 4. 1967

horizons of our young northerners. At the secondary level of the northern educational system we have observed the young students being given an opportunity not only to move from their local areas to attend other schools but to travel and visit other parts of the country. In this regard I should like to acknowledge the centennial commission's great program for youth exchanges across Canada whereby young Canadians are being given the opportunity of travelling and visiting their Canadian brothers, cousins and friends right from the east coast to the west coast and up to the Arctic ocean. In the gallery at this moment there are 24 young people who are centennial youth travellers. They are spending two weeks in the southern part of Canada and, like other young Canadians, they are visiting Expo and the House of Commons and are spending the balance of the two weeks in the Toronto area.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Before concluding my remarks regarding education I should like to draw the minister's attention, as I have many times in the past and will continue to do until we get some results, to the fact that those of us who wish to see development in the north recognize that industries based on resources, particularly mining and oil development, are the ones which have a future there. I hope that in the process of developing and adequate educational system the officials of this department together with the territorial government will take into consideration the establishment of a school of mines in the north.
One of the great difficulties we experience in the mining industry in northern Canada is the lack of a stable and adequate labour force. It seems to me if we are serious about populating this area we must use the talents and resources of our young people by encouraging them to participate in developing what will be the basic economy of northern Canada. I hope the minister and the territorial government will re-examine this question and will take the opportunity of working out with industry what is needed to carry out this development. A school of mining for northern Canada would not only assist the industries of the Yukon and the Northwest Territories but would also provide a labour force for other parts of Canada, particularly in the west. I recommend this suggestion to the minister and I hope that when he has a chance to reply he will indicate at least his concern about this particularly important matter.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I listened with interest to the comments of the hon. member for Edmonton West on the government's policy with respect to national parks. Much of what the hon. member said seemed to make sense, although in certain respects I could not help feeling in rather basic disagreement with him. I believe many members will appreciate the difficulties the minister faces in trying to administer our national parks policy in a way that (a) meets the interests of the public and (b) appears to do justice to those who over the years have held leasehold rights in our national parks.
I do not wish to aggravate the problem the minister has in this regard by advancing proposals that might appear to be, at least in the short run, popular. But it seems to me that the minister has a prime duty and obligation to see that the recreational resources of this country are developed and made available to growing numbers of people, and that no one group or clique should be able to avail itself of these resources at the expense of the general public. Of course, it is very easy to state such general requirements, but it becomes much more difficult to try to spell them out in detail and apply such a policy.
The form of leasehold which people in the national parks should be allowed to enjoy is a matter with which I am not prepared to deal at the present time. However, it occurs to me that one suggestion made by the hon. member for Edmonton West has merit, namely, that there should be no fear on the part of the government in allowing some of the cases referred to to go through the process of adjudication by the courts in order to arrive at a determination by an impartial body as to what is the right thing to do.
My personal view is that over the years numbers of people have enjoyed leasehold rights in our national parks and have had to pay annual fees, rentals, or whatever you want to call them, in an amount so small as to make it very difficult for others to understand how the government can allow this situation to continue. Therefore renegotiation is certainly required. If it should turn out that the only feasible course of action is to terminate these perpetual leases, it seems to me that the way to proceed is much the same as that in which the government now proceeds in respect of the expropriation of properties held by persons in full title or fee simple. If the parties who have held these leases can prove they have suffered concrete and substantial financial loss, methods of compensation

July 4, 1967
Supply-Indian Affairs should be worked out. If the government can proceed to expropriate property held by people in full title, why is it impossible to proceed to terminate perpetual leases in a somewhat similar manner and pay compensation for actual financial loss? Also, why can the government not proceed from there to make sure that no similar, imprudent contracts or understandings are ever again entered into?
It is my understanding that in the course of the past 18 months, or perhaps longer, the federal government has decided it would like to proceed with the establishment of second national parks in those provinces where only one national park exists at the present time. I do not know how old this policy is but I understand that the government has not got very far with the policy of establishing a second national park in several provinces.
I know that the province of Manitoba surveys and studies were undertaken by the appropriate department in consultation with the provincial authorities, to see just where in the province a second national park should be established. I understand that the present situation is one of stalemate or deadlock. This situation exists simply because the policy of the federal government is that if it is to establish a second national park the province must convey the land, without encumbrance and without condition, to the crown in the right of Canada.
On the surface there is nothing to which one can object in that policy. Certainly such land should be conveyed without encumbrance and, one would have to agree, without major condition. But I understand that one of the reasons the province of Manitoba is hesitant to transfer the land from the crown in right of the province to Canada is that the provincial authorities have reason to believe that one area, regarding which there was a tentative agreement, may very well contain mineral deposits, and they would like to enter a caveat on the conveyance of the land to the effect that some mineral prospecting and possibly exploitation will be allowed. I know that in respect of some national parks and provincial parks in other parts of Canada intergovernmental or interdepartmental ill will has been built up because parkland has been used for purposes of mineral exploitation, with deleterious effects on the area as a resource facility.
I hope the federal government will finally show some flexibility in this respect and will choose the area that was tentatively agreed upon as being suitable for a second national

park. I hope the federal government will not abandon that area and proceed to establish a second national park at the opposite end of the province. We already have a national park in northwestern Manitoba and the establishment of a second national park in that general area, which seems to be the only other possible location, would not be very logical.
I should like to refer at this time to the estimates relating to the Indian affairs branch of the department. I realize that in this regard the minister also has a very difficult portfolio to manage. Many people think that in the last two or three years advances have been made and progress is becoming more and more visible. I tend to share that opinion. On the other hand, we need not look very hard for evidence of the fact that many people consider that the Indian affairs branch has not done very much to bring about progress and improvement in the affairs of the people of Indian ancestry. Certainly in many respects there is cause for disappointment but, as I said, there are other visible signs that progress and improvement are taking place.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
I should like to express my own very firm personal view that the department is fortunate in having people who are doing good work in the field. This is not to be taken to imply that those at headquarters are not doing likewise, but my limited experience with the officials of the department in the field indicates that in working with the Indian people they are getting things done and are giving them examples of leadership and all sorts of opportunities to participate in programs of self-improvement.
I can recall visiting three classrooms at a northern Indian reserve in Manitoba about eight years ago and coming away somewhat nonplussed and puzzled by the degree of passivity among the children in the lower grades. I clearly recall thinking that there did not seem to be much prospect of these children becoming enthused about learning and it appeared that in a matter of a few years they would drop out of school. However, just three weeks ago I again visited a number of classrooms on some of these reserves in Manitoba and was literally amazed to see the extent to which the teachers of today have succeeded in instilling in the very young pupils an enthusiasm and an alertness which we would hope to find in schools everywhere. That in itself is cause for optimism because without
July 4. 1967

doubt we must still rely on education most in helping the Indian people to achieve a better standard of living.
It is not so surprising to see progress being made by the department because it has had more money to work with in recent years. It is all very well to have all sorts of programs on paper with fine ringing phrases as to what will be done, but unless the department or agency has the funds with which to give effect to all these plans on paper the whole thing is a fraud. In recent years we have been voting more money and I can say without equivocation that I feel very sure the Indian people are making very definite and decided progress, as is the department.
Some of the provinces have indicated a growing desire to participate more in the programming with respect to Indian affairs. I realize that a constitutional problem is involved and I intend to offer no further comment at the present time. However, if the provinces are really genuine in their expressed desire to enter more into the programming of Indian affairs and community development on Indian reserves, before the federal government accepts such participation it should satisfy itself that the provinces intend to allocate meaningful amounts of money for this purpose. In some respects the entry of the provinces into affairs relating to the Indian people is to be welcomed. I am all in favour of the idea, for example, that the federal government should not continue to expand the educational facilities which it offers but should rather avail itself to a greater extent of the offers made by the provinces to establish joint Indian and non-Indian schools. I believe that in this respect very tangible progress has been made in the past four or five years.
However, apart from that let us consider, for example, the community development program about which we hear from time to time from the provinces. In that connection the provincial authorities seem to have a pretty good concept on paper. Some provinces have appointed provincial civil servants as community development officers who travel to and live among the Indian people. This may sound good but I must say, having regard to all we heard about the community development program and what we had come to expect from it, there is some cause for disappointment because there is not enough money backing that program to allow it to come up to our expectations. I am afraid the federal government will be indulging in wishful 27053-140J
Supply-Indian Affairs thinking if it feels it can disengage itself from some of its programming and leave more to the provinces. However, I do not wish to prognosticate too far into the future for the simple reason that I plead ignorance.
In my humble opinion there are some areas of activity on the reserves which the Indian affairs branch should encourage rather more than it does now. I know that in recent years very definite and genuine efforts have been made to try to encourage the younger Indians especially to take on duties and responsibilities as quasi-civil servants working amoung their own people as welfare and health officers disseminating information on hygiene and other matters. I do not know to what extent this is being done officially but I am glad to say that from my own observations it seems to be working well and the department is to be commended for every effort it makes in this direction. I feel, however, we could go quite a bit further. In addition to having people on the reserves acting as health officers we could train the younger men on the reserves for purposes of law enforcement under the aegis of the R.C.M.P. I am not suggesting that they should form an organic part of the R.C.M.P. but surely it should be possible to devise a training scheme under the auspices of the R.C.M.P. whereby young men from the reserves would be taught law enforcement as it applies directly to their local situations.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
I am not sure that this comparison is a good one but I shall put it forward in any case. I am sure hon. members have heard of the efforts in the United States under the auspices of the war on poverty program, I believe, to train young men from minority groups to help keep law and order in the ghettos. I believe they go by the name of "white hats". Perhaps something along this line could be implemented in Canada in respect of the Indian reserves and the young men of Indian descent. I would be surprised if the Royal Canadian Mounted Police were not at present considering the possibility of doing something like this because I understand that they find themselves hard pressed to get enough constables and officers to allocate to the different provinces as well as look after the problems of law and order in the more northerly parts of the country and on the Indian reserves. It seems to me they would welcome such a proposition as long as it is feasible. It seems to me there would be a greater response and greater effectiveness

July 4, 1967
Supply-Indian Affairs with young people from a particular environment carrying out functions and duties which up until now have been almost exclusively carried out by civil servants. It would seem to me to be a good idea if more and more of the health officers, welfare officers and ancillary law enforcement officers were obtained through this process.
If this suggestion is followed we will be hastening the day when almost every reserve will have young Indian men and women carrying out the functions of leadership. In this way they may arrive at self-rule in the same way that men and women enjoy local selfgovernment at the municipal level. It is my understanding that the department is not fighting the process. There are some who say that the department should be disbanded or broken up, but certainly I do not subscribe to that kind of thinking. I see the minister is smiling. I really was being serious and I suggest that the functions and responsibilities of the department in connection with Indian affairs cannot be eliminated in the very near future.
No doubt some reserves are on the verge of, if not already, exercising local self-rule. I believe that one or two reserves in eastern Manitoba are already in this category. Out of the six or seven reserves I can think of offhand, one is on the verge of showing the capability of exercising complete local selfgovernment. Two or three are in various stages of preparedness. At the same time I must admit that one is some distance away from this position. Until now no effort has been successful in enabling these people to accept the normal duties and responsibilities of living in a modem society. They have followed their own way of life which did not involve them in the same kinds of problems, and so they did not learn to cope with the kinds of problems we find in our society.
However, I should like to say that while on the one hand the department is to be congratulated for its program in respect of reserve housing and town planning, it has not given priority to something that is rather elementary, the planning of house construction. When one considers the program for the complete electrification of all reserves, one finds it hard to justify why one reserve not many miles away from another that has electricity cannot get it. On some reserves there is town-site housing construction, so it is just a case of establishing priorities. I might say in that connection that despite the statements of the

band council leaders about getting electrification the department has been very sympathetic. However, they have not succeeded in getting the projects completed with the result that people on a few reservations are waiting while a few miles away money is being expended on many of the most modern amenities.
I should like to refer now to the attracting of industry. I know it is hoped that somehow, in same way, not only the reserves but most rural areas of the country will be able to attract industry. If industry were attracted to the reserve areas employment opportunities would be provided for the young people. They would then not have to move away and cut the bonds of attachment. We know that opportunities for the young in these areas are limited. There are, however, a few specific possibilities and since they are specific it seems to me the department should be interested in promoting them. I refer to specific industries, but perhaps "industry" is not the right word. I have in mind the occupation of guiding.
I know hon. members will say that there are many Indian guides, and of course there are. However, there would be a need for many more if both the federal and provincial governments were to incorporate these guides into their tourism policies. The government of Manitoba, as does the government of Canada, spends hundreds of thousands of dollars on tourist advertising in many countries, principally the United States, with considerable success. However, when people come as tourists to go fishing in our northern lakes they very often do so without hiring the services of any of the local population as guides. It seems to me there should be a lot more specific and concrete participation in the encouragement of the hiring of local Indians as guides for tourists.
In many cases certain bands or particular members of a band have a reputation as being efficient firefighters. These Indians are recruited and made use of by government agencies as firefighters. They are paid from $5 to $7 per day for this work. Five dollars to $7 a day at the very most is being paid these people for hours of work, e (4:30 p.m.)

We are trying very hard through the offices of the Indian affairs branch to open up new employment opportunities and to raise general living standards. Therefore there can be no good reason for tolerating-I use that word advisedly-the practice followed by all levels of government, and to which I think there should be a public reaction, whereby they pay Indians as little as $5 or $6 a day for firefighting. Certainly this is the case in my part of the country.
We should be doing more not only to encourage the setting up of co-ops but to assist the Indians during periods when the going is tough. We all know that work such as pulp-wood cutting and wild rice gathering, fishing and so on is cyclical and that some years are good and others are very bad. Therefore these co-ops need a little more than just initial assistance; they require sustenance during the lean periods. Since in past years we have shown no reluctance to inject a little more money into our over-all efforts to assist the Indians, we should not be quite so cautious and parsimonious about giving the co-ops which are established on many Indian reserves a little more financial assistance. We should exhibit more readiness to help them in the purchase of equipment such as tractors and tractor sleighs for hauling pulpwood, chain saws and so on. We should loosen up the purse strings a bit. If we do not assist them in this direction we shall have to do so in another. If we assist them through the provision of welfare these people are not given the opportunity to work alongside other members of society and solve their problems.
I promised to close in two minutes, Mr. Chairman, and unfortunately there are a few other things I should have liked to mention. However, if the minister takes into consideration what I have said so far I will be most grateful.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend at this time to attempt to deal with parks policy in any way but will limit my remarks to several constituency matters that are of some importance. We will await the answers to some of the questions raised by
Supply-Indian Affairs the hon. member for Edmonton West. I should like to say to the hon. member for Springfield, who has just spoken, that we are not only concerned about those who have held these park leases in the past but also about those who may hold them in the future. It is not only the recreational or conserva-tional aspects of the parks which are important. The essential services which go along with the development of the parks are also vital to the kind of development that most of us in this committee are anxious to see take place.
I would draw the attention of the minister to a matter with which I know he is familiar and which is of sufficient importance for me to impress upon him. I am referring to the David Thompson highway. The Yellowhead pass route has already been discussed this afternoon. Reference has been made to the problems that exist in Banff national park as they relate to transcontinental highway No. 1 as well as to the facilities that must be provided to meet the needs of commercial traffic. The David Thompson route, however, might well have been developed before either of these other routes had the necessary information been available to those who were responsible for laying out the original Canadian Pacific route through the mountains and later the Grand Trunk route to the north.
The David Thompson route follows the Saskatchewan River west of my home city of Red Deer, through Rocky Mountain House, through the coal mining centre of Nordegg and surrounding communities, up to the headwaters of the Saskatchewan, across the Banff-Jasper highway, up to the Howse River, over the great divide and down the Blaeberry River to a point just at the eastern foot of Rogers Pass near the town of Donald. It cuts from 80 to 90 miles off the route to the Pacific coast from any point in central Alberta or central Saskatchewan. This means that the city of Red Deer is approximately equidistant to the Pacific coast as the city of Calgary, and consequently the route saves many miles and transportation costs for all freight and tourist traffic from central Alberta and central Saskatchewan.
The provincial government of Alberta let this year the final contract for construction of that part of the highway between Nordegg and the eastern boundary of Banff national park. On August 5 the opening ceremonies are scheduled to take place at the Saskatchewan River crossing on the Banff-Jasper highway, at that point where the David

July 4. 1967
Supply-Indian Affairs Thompson route goes eastward to join up with highway 2 just north of the city of Red Deer. Not only is this route tremendously scenic, Mr. Chairman, but it is not subject to severe snowfalls in winter. Neither does it have the grades that one would normally associate with and expect to find on mountain highways.
With the construction to trans-Canada standards of grade as far as the Banff national park, the completion of the route is now a matter of urgency. Not only must the four miles be completed to join up with the Banff-Jasper road-I understand this construction is well under way at the present time-but everything possible must be done to see that the road over Howse Pass which will connect up with trans-Canada No. 1 at Donald is completed as soon as possible.
Those who support the Yellowhead route have in the past opposed the development of this route. In my opinion, in view of the volume of traffic that can be expected over the Yellowhead route, it would be of tremendous advantage to the national parks if the David Thompson route were completed because it would result in tremendous savings in transportation costs. Not only is it a much shorter route, as I have already indicated, but the construction of the road is comparatively easy. The grades involved are very minor indeed having regard to the type of mountainous country through which the proposed highway passes.
I therefore hope the department will not wait for the government of British Columbia to build its 28.5 miles, I believe it is, of the road from the western border of Banff national park, but will take the initiative and develop the route through the very narrow waist of the park at House Pass.

Not only would it cut some 80 or 90 miles off the distance to the Pacific coast but it also offers the advantage of attracting much of the commercial highway transportation which now goes through Banff national park by way of Banff and Lake Louise, bypassing altogether the bottleneck presented by that difficult road and the costly type of construction involved between Field and Golden. I believe much of the commercial transportation which now passes through the Banff bottleneck and which has been the cause of much of the dissension in connection with park policies would prefer to take the new route instead of No. 1 highway which it presently follows,
IMr. Thompson.]
bearing in mind that the distance to be travelled is shorter and the grades are less steep. Banff park narrows to a distance of only 20 miles approximately where the Thompson route crosses it, resulting in less interference with recreational development. I would remind the minister that this heavy commercial traffic has been among the causes of the difficulties which now exist in the park, and if these could be alleviated by providing an alternative commercial route the minister would face fewer problems than he does at the present time.
From the Saskatchewan River crossing going east this highway makes a figure eight out of the circular route from Calgary to Edmonton through Red Deer and from Edmonton to Jasper and Jasper to Lake Louise and eastward to Banff and Calgary. It would be extremely attractive to tourists because they would only have to travel half the distance to see some of the most spectacular mountain scenery there is anywhere in the world, whether on the northern or the southern half of this route now being created.
I trust the minister will be able to have the first four miles of incoming road between the Jasper-Banff road and the eastern park boundary completed by August 5 for normal travel, together with the necessary bridge across the river at the park boundary. With most of the highway already completed, a park gate is needed very quickly because the volume of traffic passing into the park is already large. A new park entrance would facilitate the work which the employees of the parks branch must perform in controlling traffic and collecting entrance fees. It would also assist tourists travelling through the area. I believe budgetary provision has been made for this expenditure for at least one year, if not for two.
Another important need concerns the provision of facilities to-handle tourist traffic at this particular point. There is already a need for vastly expanded camping facilities, and provision must likewise be made for the building of motels. Anyone who has travelled through the park between Jasper and Lake Louise appreciates that there is extreme pressure on existing facilities. Although much has already been done to increase facilities I believe there is need for a crash program. If the increase in the last two or three years is any indication of what will happen in the next two or three years, great attention must be paid to the provision of both campsites and motels. Action is needed now, without delay, since this highway is to open on August 5.
