The highway department of the government of Alberta is to be congratulated on the vision it has shown in the development of its portion of the new highway. The potential of this highway does not just involve those who live along the route nearly as much as it does the development of the over-all tourist industry in Banff and Jasper, and the consequences which will flow from a more economical route over the mountains, affecting all western Canada.
I have drawn the attention of the minister to the importance of these developments and to the need for extra effort to be made to provide facilities for handling a growing tourist influx into the parks through this new entrance, but I emphasize as well as the desirability of completing this road from the Saskatchewan River crossing so as to join No. 1 highway at Donald station.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to thank the minister for his co-operation in supplying the buffalo meat for the biggest buffalo picnic in Canada's history. Had it not been for the co-operation of the hon. gentleman's department, that picnic would certainly have been a failure. I want to go on record as thanking both the hon. gentleman and his department for their part in its success.
One of the most important duties which the minister has assumed is responsibility for heading the department of Indian affairs. I happen to think it is among the most important departments in the government, though very often it fails to get the attention it deserves. Our Indian people are the senior citizens of Canada and the fact that the twentieth century has left them far behind is no excuse for a rich young country like Canada, which has profited from living in their land, continuing to neglect their important and pressing needs. I do not think we shall ever reach the Indian people and enable them to take the place in Canadian life they deserve and be as prosperous, as well educated, as well placed in our industries and professions as they should be unless we really get to understand them. They are a proud race, like all the families of mankind. They have just the same capabilities and just the same desires as all of us. But they have been left high and dry. I shall say nothing in recrimination; I will try to make a positive contribution.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
Let us forget the errors of the past and press on with a positive answer to the Indian problem. We have to help the Indian restore
Supply-Indian Affairs his pride in himself. If we can do that all the other problems will fall into their proper places. The most important thing we could do would be to appoint a deputy minister of Indian or Eskimo origin. We can find such a man if we look for him. There are such men in our country as the Rev. Ahenakiew, an Anglican minister who is a full-bloded Cree. We have several Indians who are versatile enough to belong to the R.C.M.P. The minister has several members in his own department who are excellent men. There is Mr. Kelly who went to New Zealand and studied the native problem there. There is Mr. William Bull of Alberta who on several occasions has been elected chief of the Goodfish reserve. There is Mr. Steinhauer who is very prominent in northern Alberta on the Saddle Lake Reserve. He at one time ran in an election for member of parliament. I look forward to the day when we will have several members of parliament of native origin.
The old pride which the Indians had and which lies dormant in them must be brought to the fore if they are to have any hope. It is not just a question of money. We can spend hundreds of millions of dollars but as long as we are paternal with these people, not friendly, understanding and co-operative, the money will go down the drain.
It is almost useless to try to raise the standard of living of an Indian on a reserve without raising the standard of living of the whole tribe. We can send an Indian boy to school and put him through high school, but when he goes back to the reserve later he is a whitewashed crow. His very vocabulary will make him unpopular with his fellows. Unless we educate all the Indians as much as we can we are merely giving some of them the white man's ways. Unless they want those ways it is useless to ram them down their throats. Probably many people within the sound of my voice think that all the Indians need is homes like ours with hardwood floors and Crane plumbing. But Indians might be happier in good tents, temporarily at least, if the tents were warm and well stocked. They might be happier to spend money on clothes, what they call fine feathers.
I suppose some hon. members may say, "All right, if you know these people so well, what is your solution"? I am speaking primarily of western Canada because I know that area. Some of the reserves there have the most excellent ranching land in Canada but in many cases it is going to waste. I could take members out there and show them large stretches of virgin prairie owned by Indians.

July 4. 1967
Supply-Indian Affairs Yet today at a time when beef cattle are at a premium there are no cattle on these lands or, if there are, they are owned by white men. The Indians are beginning to understand that if this grazing land can make money for white men there is no reason why it should not make money for Indians.
I suggest that we go to the Indian, consult with him, find out how much of the white man's ways he wants, how much discipline he will supply himself and by communal effort. We should give them whatever they want and allow them to be their own administrators. Indians, like any other branch of the human family, will take pride in doing things on their own. Some hon. members may try to downgrade this idea by saying it is nothing but a form of communism. But perhaps Indians need a form of communal living because they are not yet ready for the twentieth century.
We should try to restore the Indians' pride in themselves. We should provide them with a workable plan for a way of life close to their old accepted way of life when they lived off buffalo herds or by individual trapping in the woods. If some Indians want to be ranchers we should help them to become ranchers. If some of them want to remain in the woods perhaps we could work them into the tourist industry as guides.
Many Indians are very capable with their hands. They are efficient at manufacturing in the home. They are certainly capable of maintaining outboard motors. They like fine feathers. These Indians would be at a premium if they dressed in their own beautiful native costumes made of hand-tanned leather, which is still available and which we can help them to get. If they did this and acted as guides, then our American relatives and European visitors would get some of the colour of our rich Canadian culture.
The Indians must have autonomy. They are taught from the cradle to hate us. This is a negative approach. But I do not think they would hate us if we really extended to them the kind of friendship we would expect if we were in their place. If we did that they might teach their children to love us and eventually accept the best part of the white man's ways.
Where Indians have had economic security they have progressed. They are capable of all the skills of the white man. They are just as capable as the white man with their hands and their heads. As hon. members know, Caughnawaga Indians get premium wages in steel construction work. Their native skill in

trotting along logs through the forest gave them sure footing. Now they raise their children to expect to be somebody when they reach their later teens. They have pride in themselves. They trot along the high steel of skyscrapers in New York, Montreal, Edmonton and Winnipeg and they show us that the red man is truly noble, like the rest of the human race, when he has a chance.
I hope the minister will pay heed to this plea on behalf of the Indians. There are legal hitches. The Indian Act needs to be revised. The treaties need to be revised. Of course the Indians are afraid to touch the treaties because they feel the treaties were not kept in the past. Again I beg that the Indian claims commission, promised for 50 years, be brought into being. Let it be a commission for the Indians, not merely the enlargement of another arm of government to make jobs for white men. Let it be a commission which will correct those errors we committed when we did not keep our side of the treaties. Such a commission can help bring about a new deal for Indians, one that is long overdue. But that commission will not work if the Indians feel it is just another piece of bureaucracy and not an honest attempt at friendly co-operation.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
I have read one or two draft bills. One of them contained a suggestion that there should be a commission made up of three appointees. One member of the commission would be a member of the judiciary, one would be an appointee of the government and the third would be an appointee of the Indians. The subclause immediately following said that the Indian appointee would be subject to removal at the whim of both houses of parliament. This would be a mistake which would negate the whole effectiveness of this new commission. The Indian appointee must be subject only to the wishes of the Indians themselves. We have had at least 100 years of delay and, if this should cause further delay, a few more months would not make any difference. This man must be an Indian appointee and his tenure of office must be subject only to the wishes of the Indians themselves. Canada is a great and large country. There are many tribes involved. I believe it would be well nigh impossible to pick any one Indian and say that he represents the native people of this country. If we were to pick a Mohawk, perhaps the west coast Indians of British Columbia would think that he would know little about their ancient fishing rights.
July 4, 1967

Therefore I suggest that when this commission is set up it should be a flexible so far as the Indian appointee is concerned. By all means let an independent judge sit as the chairman of the commission, and the government, of course, would have to have an efficient civil servant who knows the act and the conditions under which the government has worked over the last 20 years or so. However, so far as the Indian appointee is concerned I suggest that this commission, which certainly will have to move across the country in order to deal with these problems one at a time, should accept an appointee from the Mohawk tribe or from the family of tribes as the case may be.
It might be possible to get the Bloods, the Peigans and the Sarcee to agree on an appointee but so far as the Crees are concerned I believe the great family of Crees should have its own appointee. In this way the Indian appointee would be one who would know the problems of the Indians in a particular part of the country. I have heard that one of the reasons the commission has not yet been set up is that there is not unanimity among the Indians. If this is what is causing the bottleneck now, it can be avoided by making the appointment of the Indian representative flexible.
Some people have said that it would be dangerous to open up all the treaties. It has been said that this might cost us a good deal of money. Well, Canada is a country which always pays its debts. This is something which should concern the claims commission. If we do owe these people money, larger pieces of territory, or considerable mineral rights which they have been unable to use, then let us establish this commission and find out what the facts are. I am sure that when all the facts are placed before us we will not hesitate to pay these people what we owe them. I am sure we will not hesitate to place at their disposal some of the tremendous resources of this country in order to bring them in this second century of Canada's history to the place of honour which because of their friendly acceptance of us they so rightfully deserve.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my remarks at this time will be very brief. They stem particularly from the fact that our national and historic resources come under the jurisdiction of the minister whose estimates we are discussing at the moment. More particularly my participation at this time is, of 27053-141
Supply-Indian Affairs course motivated by the very welcome announcement made by the minister during the question period when, in answer to a question placed on the order paper some time earlier by the hon. member for Essex West, he reiterated the statement made in March that the resting places or graves of the fathers of confederation would be considered as historical sites and consequently would be eligible for some type of financial assistance from the department concerned.
Before I speak directly and specifically about this problem. I should like to pay tribute to this division of the department. Living as I do on the island of Montreal I have had no direct contact with the work of this section of the minister's department in latter years, but I recall with a certain degree of affection the existence of the park which we used to call simply the Plains of Abraham situated in the city of Quebec, and the role that park plays in that communiry. I recall, of course, the period of my life when I lived in the city of Quebec between the ages of 10 and 17. That period coincided with the depression years. The few persons here who have lived through the depression years will know that many Canadians compensated for the lack of money by using a little initiative in utilizing their leisure time. High in the order of priority in this regard in the city of Quebec were the Plains of Abraham. That park is a tremendous credit to the department.
It is perhaps true that the Plains of Abraham are known best for their historical significance, but to the residents of Quebec, the Plains, which is the name we used for the park, was a meeting place where the citizens could enjoy picnics and otherwise make good use of their leisure time by using the park for recreation. However, like most people, during my early days I paid little or no attention or gave any credit to the battlefields commission which is charged with the responsibility of maintaining the park. I suppose that like most citizens of Quebec I assumed the park was maintained in some miraculous fashion by the city of Quebec or the provincial authorities or was endowed by private interests. It was, of course, only when I grew up and became a little more interested in politics and a little more aware of things around me that I realized that this place of beauty was maintained by a particular department of the federal government.
I think it is to the everlasting credit of successive governments, both Conservative and Liberal, that the overriding policy in the

Supply-Indian Affairs park has been to maintain the beauty of its sitting. This park has been a tremendous boon to the tourist trade. It is one of the foremost tourist attractions. Many hundreds and thousands of tourists who will visit Quebec, during our centennial year, will of course visit this park. So I should like to congratulate the minister.
I note in the estimates of the department that very little increase has been designated for this branch. This puzzles me a bit because I believe that like many others it is suffering as a result of increased salaries and the increased cost of maintaining parks and sites.
Today, as a result of a question asked by the hon. member for Essex West, the minister repeated the assurance he gave the house on March 15 that something will be done about the graves of the fathers of confederation which in many instances are badly in need of restoration. My interest in the subject arose quite naturally as a result of representations made to me by various organizations on the island of Montreal, particularly the St. Patrick's Society. I was prevailed upon to ask whether there was some department of government which would assume the moral and financial responsibility of looking after the resting places of those wonderful men who 100 years ago had the vision of forming this country known as Canada.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
Like that of most backbenchers, my route to the very kindly and sympathetic ear of the minister was a long and tortuous one. I commenced my approach rather naively by going to the Minister of Public Works. After many months of sympathetic correspondence we mutually arrived at the conclusion that I was dealing with the wrong department. After six months of rather harrowing experience I then rather naively transferred my efforts to the centennial commission, presuming that in a country which was about to celebrate its centennial the resting place of Thomas D'Arcy McGee should be more important than the assassination of Abraham Lincoln. When one watches television on Sunday night and observes programs such as the Walt Disney program or others from the United States to which we are exposed culturally in Canada, it is quite easy to understand why the average youngster in Canada is familiar with the exploits of Abraham Lincoln but knows relatively little about the father of confederation who was assassinated within sight of the parliament buildings.

July 4, 1967
I was informed on several occasions that while my project was a very suitable one centennial funds for this type of endeavour were not provided by the federal government but rather were the joint responsibility of the federal, provincial and civic authorities. I started over again and approached these three levels of government with the hope that some financial assistance could be provided for this project in which I was interested. After many months of letter writing I was again assured that my project was a very wonderful and touching one for centennial year but unfortunately the funds for this type of project had been exhausted and I was from 60 to 90 days too late.
It was at this time the suggestion was advanced by the then minister without portfolio, the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, that I turn my efforts in the direction of the minister of northern affairs, whose estimates we are considering at this moment. I am very pleased to say I found it much easier and more simple to convince him of the validity of my case than any of the other avenues which I explored for some 12 to 15 months.
Let me leave this suggestion with the minister in the hope that he may expand a little when his opportunity comes later in the evening to answer some of the questions. On March 15 the minister announced that after a series of meetings with that branch of his department that I refer to as the historic branch but which is actually the natural historic and resources branch, it was felt normal and natural that the graves or resting places of the fathers of confederation should be considered as historic sites. I am sure hon. members will agree with that decision, particularly in view of the fact that we are discovering perhaps for the first time what it means to be a Canadian.
The spontaneous efforts of the people of Canada during this last week in breaking away from or putting aside our inferiority complex, make it more important that we should realize and cherish the efforts of the fathers of confederation. The fact that this country is only 100 years old makes it possible for us to do something to remember these people. Their speeches are recorded in Hansard and there are other ways of remembering them. But it does seem to me as it did to the minister that we could do something else such as providing assistance to an organization such as the St. Patrick's Society of Montreal to restore to its proper condition the resting place of Thomas D'Arcy McGee.
July 4, 1967

In his remarks of March 15, in which the minister announced that the department was prepared to render financial assistance for the restoration of these resting places, he created some puzzlement by his use of the phrase "financial assistance". That term implies that somebody or some corporation or society must exist to assist financially. How or who do you help financially in those cases where no society or corporation exists? In the case of the Thomas D'Arcy McGee project fortunately, there is a body in existence that can be helped financially. I refer, of course, to the St. Patrick's Society.
It is not difficult to visualize that in other instances there are no such societies. I have made representations to the minister asking him to elaborate further in defining "financial assistance", because it seems to me this is the key phrase in his statement of March 15. I suspect the minister will want to discuss this point and I hope that when he does he will point out that financial assistance can vary from one project to another from 10 per cent to 50 per cent or perhaps up to 100 per cent depending on how elaborate or simple the project is.
In the particular case of Thomas D'Arcy McGee I am happy to say that McGee sat as a member of the two major parties which existed at that time. We were not faced with the curse of socialism 100 years ago. In any event, Thomas D'Arcy McGee entered the house as a Liberal, although unfortunately in a moment of weakness he became a Conservative. I notice that an hon. member on the front benches of the opposition removed his glasses after hearing that remark. In a serious vein, Thomas D'Arcy McGee was a great father of confederation and certainly the complete cost of the project I have in mind should be absorbed by the minister's department, I hope that at the first opportunity the minister will re-assure me.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, everyone who has held the portfolio held by the present incumbent has realized a great sense of responsibility. I know that his predecessor, the hon. member for Brandon-Souris, was keenly interested in the north and its development. He came to know the area and to love it. He did great things here in Ottawa and elsewhere to create a feeling of development in the north. I realize this very well because in 1961 when a ceremony was held at the opening of the Pine Point railway the hon. member for Brandon-Souris climbed on a caterpillar tractor to carry out the usual ceremonial functions. We 27053-1415
Supply-Indian Affairs saw him disappear over a hill, heading north, and it took some time to find out how far he
had gone and bring him back.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: They could not stop the machinery.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
I am advised, Mr. Chairman, that they could not stop the machinery. I think there is a great opportunity for a minister who holds this portfolio to do what I believe one British prime minister said when asked what his achievements were. He was referring to North America and he said, "I have helped call into being a new world to redress the balance of the old." I know the present minister feels this way. God knows, there is enough to redress in the balance of the old world and the old part of Canada.
There are a great many things to be done. I shall not go into detail at this stage because I have made my views known from time to time. However, I think it is of interest to point out that Dr. Deutsch, chairman of the Economic Council of Canada has become very interested in the question of the north and northern development. He made two trips to the territories in company, I believe, with the minister and some of his officials. He stopped on the way at the town of Peace River. Unfortunately I was not able to meet him. The interest of Dr. Deutsch in the north is pointed up in the third report of the Economic Council of Canada. I think this should give the minister an opportunity to do a little arm-twisting with his colleagues, particularly the Minister of Finance, who sits quite close to him, when the occasion arises. The problem is in getting the money and spending it in the right places.
I have made one suggestion to the minister and I make it again. I believe it would be very suitable, particularly this year, if the minister would take the initiative and convene an international meeting of those nations which have jurisdiction in the north, that is, Canada, the United States in right of Alaska, the Soviet union and the Scandinavian countries. I suggest it would be very appropriate to convene such a meeting in Yellowknife. Representatives of these countries should be brought together to consider ways and means of peacefully exchanging and pooling information dealing with northern development. We in Canada have made progress in this regard. The Russians have made progress in areas in which we perhaps have not been able to. But I believe that in a spirit of detente this is an excellent area in

July 4, 1967
Supply-Indian Affairs which these people can come together and pool their information.
In certain areas there is no question of security or classification. There is a common interest in the world to bring into a reasonable degree of economic development those parts of the north which are suitable for occupation, exploitation and development. I do not think there is any question about this. We know that for different reasons the Russians have been able to establish cities of a million or half a million people far to the north of our largest settlement of Yellowknife. There are, of course, geographical and political reasons for their being able to do this.
I believe it is now common knowledge that in Russia there is a system of incentives which persuades people, particularly the young, to go to these areas. On the North American continent today the two nations, in particular the United States, are spending billions and billions of dollars in space exploration and development. This is very essential and a start had to be made in this field. However, it seems to me it is also very essential that we be prepared to devote a reasonable part of our national economy for the purpose of seeing what parts of the north can be developed and, where there are resources, what we can do with them.
I have said over and over again that a country that concentrates its resources and population in one limited area, as we are doing in Canada, is looking for trouble. The cost of policing, sanitation, building houses and educating children grows increasingly higher in these areas. There is an increasingly large number of problems in connection with these areas. Now is the time to work together with other nations and lay out a plan for the development and utilization of the north.
We know it will not be too many years before parts of the world, particularly this continent, will be running short of certain strategic materials. I do not know to what extent the Paley report has been followed or to what extent people in the United States are examining it. But I remember there was a feeling a number of years ago that certain strategic materials required for industrial use and development would be in short supply. It is the tendency of human nature to wait too long to take the steps which need to be taken to see that there is a rounding off and a normal development in this regard. This applies to our continent and this country. I hope fMr. Baldwin.]
the minister will give some thought to convening such an international meeting as a preliminary step to solving these problems. The increasing use of commodity pipe lines and changes in trade development and the exchange of goods will in the not too distant future, I believe, bring us to a period of time when the north will have great strategic importance, not necessarily in terms of defence strategy but in terms of trade and communications.
I listened with interest to the hon. member for Athabasca who spoke about our Indians and the Indian problem. I do not think we have an Indian problem, although it is often referred to as such. There are a number of Indian people who have problems. There are a number of Indian bands which have problems. This is why it is extremely difficult for us, sitting here in Ottawa, to formulate proposals on a broad, national scale which will be suitable for application to the Indian people in all parts of Canada. I suggest that we must have-and I believe the department is moving in this direction-a great measure of decentralization in order to give to the officials in the various areas, the superintendents and regional directors, a greater measure of authority and independence so they will be able to apply the general policies laid down in Ottawa broadly in a way which will best benefit their districts. We in Ottawa have a tendency to feel, when we appropriate $10 million or $20 million for a certain project, that the money will trickle down and will ultimately be used by individuals in those areas that we believe need improving. But this is not always the case. All too often the way the money is used is a matter of discretion on the part of independent civil servants who are on the firing line.
From what I have learned I believe that the policy I suggest has been applied to some extent but I should like to see it accentuated. It means getting the very best people that we can in these areas, people who will be responsible for dealing with the Indians, and giving them not carte blanche but at least within certain limits the right to modify policies according to circumstances in a way which will best benefit the Indian peoples with whom they are dealing and the areas where they live.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
I should like to give the minister an example of what I mean. In the community of Hay Lakes, with which I think the minister is familiar-it is not too far from the famous
July 4, 1967

Rainbow lake oil area-some years ago a white man was engaged by the band council to inaugurate a system of cutting logs and get the Indians involved in this work. He was to teach them the essential mechanical trades and help them develop a self-contained enterprise. This man made very substantial progress in his first year and a half of operation. He was able to provide the oil companies with lumber much cheaper than they could get it flown in.
At that time there was no highway into this area. I flew in there on two or three occasions and I talked to him. At one time it looked as if he would be able to set in motion an economic operation which would give year round employment to the 40 or 50 men who made up the majority of the heads of households in this area. Unfortunately, because of red tape and restrictions some difficulties developed. Eventually the man had to leave because of problems which arose with the local superintendent as a result of difficulties with the lines of communication in getting the equipment which was necessary, and so far as I know nothing more was done. Here was a situation where 40 or 50 adult Indians and their families would have been able to initiate, develop and continue an economic program which would have given employment to a large percentage of potential wage earners in the district. These are the sort of opportunities for which we should look, particularly in the northern part of Alberta, in the territories and in the northern part of Saskatchewan.
As a result of the sudden influx of people in connection with oil exploration and the development of the oil industry, the traditional sources or earning a living such as fishing and trapping have been taken away. These people have been suddenly exposed to civilization. They are untrained, unprepared and incapable of earning a living. At this time there is a special urgency about many of these cases.
However, I feel that our great problem lies with the education of the Indian children. In my part of the world in northern Alberta the Grouard vocational training school has been providing education to many Indian children who might otherwise have dropped out of school. I had the good fortune of welcoming three of these children to Ottawa not long ago. The boys had come here to study forestry and mechanical trades such as welding and the girls were taking beauty counselling and nurses' aides courses. It is my belief that in normal circumstances these children would
Supply-Indian Affairs have dropped out of school had it not been for this vocational training scheme.
This is the kind of thing on which the government should concentrate. We must bring these people one stage further and give them the opportunity to take one more step up the economic and social ladder. It is a difficult and heartbreaking problem and I know very well what is involved, but I urge the minister, if he happens to be in that district, to go to Grouard, look at the vocational training school there and see the Indian and white children working together at their desks and in the machine shops. I think these children will be far better able to enter into the economic and social life of this country than their fathers and grandfathers were.
The hon. member for Athabasca spoke about the Indian claims commission. This is a very difficult problem. If the claims commission were to be invested with the complete authority that is required to deal equitably-I stress that word-with all of the justified complaints of the Indian people and if this were to bring remunerative results, it would mean a tremendous amount of money. Not long ago I read about a decision of the supreme court of the United States according to which Florida belongs to a tribe of Indian people who under that judgment are entitled to take over Florida. I do not know what they would do with Miami Beach and the gambling houses there. However, if a court were to look at some of the original treaties and agreements made between representatives of the crown and Indian representatives over the last 50 or 60 years, it would be compelled to come up with a decision that these were fraudulent agreements obtained under false pretences and on the basis of promises which were never kept. If these treaties were to be interpreted in the light of modem conditions they would all have to be declared illegal. However, we as practical people know this is not possible.
In any event, we know that we have made great progress in this country, and what we want to do now is to give the Indian people an opportunity to participate in the reaping of the benefits which should and must be made available to them. This is the conundrum which will face the minister and the government when they come to enact the Indian claims commission legislation. They will have to consider on what terms it should be drafted. I would suggest that before the judgment of the government becomes final the minister might give thought to letting a committee look at this whole matter and

July 4, 1967
Supply-Indian Affairs make suggestions and proposals regarding it. Of course its terms of reference would have to be drawn up fairly carefully. This is a matter in which the work of the standing committee might be of benefit to the government before the legislation is drawn and brought down.
I was present and saw the Indians from Quebec perform their folk dances on June 30. I know that Her Majesty visited the pavilion of the Indian peoples at Expo during the course of her sojourn there yesterday. I am sure she read the messages left there by the Indian people regarding the injustices which they feel have been meted out to them. These are not injustices which this generation alone must sustain but injustices over a period of the last 100 years for which the people of Canada must bear the responsibility. As I watched the Indian people dancing here and as I read about Her Majesty's visit to the Indian pavilion I thought that something must be done now so that when we pat ourselves on the back and tell ourselves what wonderful fellows we are and what a wonderful birthday party we are having we will realize that we are not entitled to that feeling without accepting some degree of blame and involving ourselves in a meaningful program to help these people.
The minister has made some announcements with respect to housing and I know that the government is heading in the right direction. But time is not on our side. I would hope that all members of the house will resolve, in a nonpartisan way and without allowing their views to be swayed by political consideration, that at this time when we are celebrating our centennial something more meaningful will be done to bring the level of the original settlers of Canada, the Indian people, up to a stage where they can share and will have the right to share, as they should have had before, in a far more material way in the birthday party which we are having in Canada.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to endorse the appeal made to the minister by the hon. member for Peace River so far as it concerned the decentralization of Indian affairs services. Since I came to Ottawa I have witnessed the federal government wallowing incompetently in areas where it had invaded both provincial and municipal authority. In view of the fact that the Indian problem is not just a general one involving national Indian policy across the country but one concerning Indians in specific locations, a

program of decentralization and concentration in these areas instead of trying to deal with the statistical average Indian would be of great benefit to the Indians of Canada. I think
we want to get more return for the effort and energy we are extending in trying to help the Indians.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
There are, it seems to me, three types of problems connected with the Indians. They can be loosely categorized as, first, urban problems related to those Indians who have migrated from reserves to cities and those Indians who live on reserves adjacent to cities. Then we have the rural based Indians who live near rural townsites. Third, we have the Indians of the far northern areas. It is the latter two types with which I should like to deal for a few minutes because many of the people who inhabit my constituency belong in these categories.
We have found a variety of difficulties in trying to bring the Indians up to a more equitable standard of living. We must, I believe, provide them with an opportunity to make a place for themselves in Canadian society. I have found the Indians, generally speaking, to be interested in earning their own way. A great many of them resent the welfare handouts which we give them. As a matter of fact, some of them go so far as to say that we give these welfare handouts much more easily than we give them the tools and education they need to make their own way.
I have an example of this which I should like to mention at this time. One of the few natural resources available to the Indians for exploitation in northern Ontario is fish. Indians can fish both summer and winter. There is a company in Keewatin called Shoal Lake Fisheries Limited which set out to attempt to exploit the fish resources of Lake of the Woods in the northwest part of Ontario. Originally it supplied the Indians with capital equipment in the form of nets, outboard motors, boats and all the other necessary paraphernalia. The capital amount was to be paid back out of the earnings the Indians made from fishing.
Several things have gone wrong with this plan. First of all, there has been an out and out failure by the Department of Transport to enforce its own regulations concerning commercial aircraft in the north. There are a good many freebooters, people who own small aircraft and who on occasion will take a flight up north looking for an Indian who is fishing.
July 4, 19G7

When they spot one they will land and offer to buy his fish for which they pay cash. They take the fish and Shoal Lake Fisheries has to take a severe loss because it is not able to buy the fish that the company equips the Indians to catch. In addition, the company cannot collect any of the money invested in capital equipment.
There are other areas in which the department of Indian affairs has taken a different attitude. I have a letter here from which I should like to quote. It was written to the Ontario Development Corporation at Toronto by the president of Shoal Lake Fisheries Limited. The company is having a great deal of difficulty finding the necessary capital to expand because their accounts receivable are so great. This, in turn, is related to the fact they are unable to collect the money which they put out for equipment because they have not been able to get the fish which the Indians have been catching. The situation is simply this. They were advised by the department of Indian affairs to cease providing the Indians with capital equipment. The Indian affairs department claimed they would provide the capital equipment because they had funds put aside for this purpose. The letter reads in part:
We would like to point out that this statement regarding the availability of funds is probably quite true, however, no one has advised the Indians nor our organization as to how these funds may be put in the hands of the potential fisherman.
Then the letter goes on to deal with a meeting held recently in Toronto. One of the local Indian chiefs, along with some officials from the Ontario Development Corporation, met with officials of the department of Indian affairs. I should like to read from the letter again:
At this meeting Mr. Greene-
He is an Indian chief.
-stated that he was unable to obtain government financing which would enable him to fish commercially.
That is the end of the statement. Chief Greene is a chief at the Shoal Lake reserve which is adjacent to Lake of the Woods. If I may, I should like to continue the quotation:
If we discontinued advances completely, a number of Indians would not be in a position to fish commercially and again would rely on welfare funds (more readily obtainable than fishing equipment from the department of Indian Affairs), as a means of livelihood.
So there seems to be a certain ambivalence here in departmental policy. On the one hand, they protect the Indians in a certain area and
Supply-Indian Affairs they protect the fish production. They see that the Indians receive a just price. The department takes no loss. At the same time, they expose a private entrepreneur to all the risks in developing Indian fishing when he is at the same time helping the Indian. The company has to take all the risks and has no protection at all. It seems to me that this is the type of operation that the Indian affairs branch should step into. I agree that in many cases it is necessary for the department to educate the Indians in modern, twentieth century money management. At the same time, it seems to me unreasonable to discriminate against this company, the only fish processor in northwestern Ontario. I bring these facts to the attention of the minister respectfully in the hope he might look into them and rectify the situation. I think it can be done without too much difficulty.
There is another matter which I hesitate to raise because it is a very sensitive one. I certainly hope hon. members will not misinterpret what I am going to say now. This point involves particularly the town of Kenora which, as hon. members will recall, was the scene of an Indian march about two years ago. This occurred on November 15, 1965 and was the subject of my first speech in the House of Commons. Since that time Kenora has become an even greater centre for the Indians than it was before. I refer to the very difficult question of policing. The Indians treat Kenora much in the same way as people from other rural areas treat a big city. They come in and have a good time. This leads to certain consequences. In the wintertime the police are absolutely necessary to prevent the Indian people from dying of exposure. In summer the police are just as necessary. The Indians themselves have suggested that one way around the bind of policing costs would be for the Indian affairs department, in co-operation with the municipality, to hire Indian policemen.
Two things would be accomplished in this way. Attention would be directed to one of the problems and the town would be assisted in financing this project. The tax base of the town is extremely limited, so it does require some assistance in dealing with this problem. Since the Indians themselves have recommended this idea of providing an Indian police force, it seems to me that the Indian affairs branch would be well advised to investigate this suggestion to ascertain if some form of arrangement could be worked out. I think it has certain possibilities and I should

July 4. 1967
Supply-Indian Affairs like to see serious consideration given to it. The problem the town of Kenora faces-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question? Can he tell us whether there are any Indians on the Kenora police force?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
To my knowledge there are none. There was some talk, if memory serves me correctly, of an attempt to hire one some time ago. However, there was no one available who could take the police course. In all honesty, I think they are looking for some relief from the pressure of providing this assistance. They are also looking for some opportunity for the Indians to bring about improvements themselves.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
The town of Kenora, the town of Fort Frances, the district of Red Lake and the town of Sioux Lookout all have serious difficulties in dealing with this problem because they are all urban centres for the Indians living in the neighbourhood. They do not have the finances to provide all the services required of them for the people living within their own municipal borders let alone deal with the problem they are facing as centres for a large indigenous Indian population.
However, these centres have been trying to make some progress and in the town of Kenora, through the facilities offered by the University of Manitoba adult education branch, the authorities were able to sponsor a series of ten lectures given by distinguished anthropologists and other experts on Indian affairs to explain to the people of Kenora, who have never faced this problem before, exactly what was going on, the type of crosscultural conflicts that were beginning, why the Indian was as he was, and what were the possibilities for change. Much to the surprise of everyone concerned with the project the response was overwhelming. The sponsoring committee was caught without sufficient seats and without a sufficiently large hall a number of times.
The second thing they did was to set up a branch of the Ontario Alcohol Research Foundation which now has some very meagre facilities in the way of attempting to provide counselling and assistance to those Indians who run afoul of the juice of the grape. They have run into problems of financing and the reason for this goes back to the time of the march on the town of Kenora. Because of the confused conditions which existed at that tilme, a number of commitments were made

without prior consultation with the proper authorities and the local people to their credit went ahead without getting formal written confirmation. As a consequence they arrived at a point where they had the facilities but did not have any money with which to operate them. They have had their problem solved for a year or two now, and I must congratulate the minister because his department is now providing more assistance than it did before. But they still have a problem in trying to deal with the situation as a whole.
Nevertheless, Mr. Chairman, progress is being made by the local association. We have in Kenora another institution known as the Kenora Fellowship Centre, though there is a drawback so far as provision of assistance from the federal government through the department of Indian Affairs is concerned in that it has the stigma of having a religious affiliation. I understand that the policy of the department now is that any body which has a religious affiliation is looked upon with very deep suspicion, and in the end result, generally speaking, any financial assistance given is very minimal or none at all. We are attempting to broaden the base of this fellowship centre. I believe its membership is 50 per cent Indian and 50 per cent white, and the church in question is the Presbyterian church.
I do not particularly like this policy of the Indian affairs branch in discriminating against religious associations in this way. The simple fact is that, while the House of Commons did nothing for the Indians for many years, it was the religious associations that ahnost singlehandedly provided any kind of services to the Indians. The House of Commons has now finally decided to look into the matter of providing some assistance but it is trying to sweep out the old crew with a new broom, and I think this is unfair. The department should be providing some form of assistance to the Kenora Fellowship Centre because here is a body that has been set up on a community basis without any assistance from the federal department of Indian affairs yet because it has a religious affiliation it is being discriminated against, and so far no assistance has been forthcoming.
I understand I have a few minutes left, Mr. Chairman, so I should like to say a few words about program 5. We have been able to utilize program 5 to a great extent in my constituency. While this has caused a great deal of discontent in certain quarters as well as a great deal of criticism, I think the over-all effect of the program has been most beneficial
July 4, 1967

both to the Indians and to the communities concerned.
In the first place it does away with a great deal of the discrimination the Indians have had to face in that the Indians are involved in this program along with other people. It has had a great effect in providing the Indian for the first time with a great deal of self-confidence. He has been able to go into the classroom and compete with white people and has been able to find out that he is their equal. While you and I, Mr. Chairman, may admit this, the Indian has not admitted it as a fact. I think he has always considered himself to be a little below the white man, so this program has had an impact in increasing his self-confidence. It has had an impact in making him aware that the world is a much larger place than he thought.
It has also provided the opportunity to help us integrate the Indians into our communities. Like all integration this will be difficult. There are a lot of rough edges and there will be many incidents. But it is coming, it is worth while, and I for one look forward to it.
I understand that the minister of Indian affairs will be coming to the Kenora area on August 19 to attend the centennial celebrations of the Indians who come under treaty No. 3 in northwestern Ontario. I am looking forward to welcoming him at that time, and I am also looking forward to introducing him to the many people who are engaged in these local community activities that deal with Indian affairs.
The other point I should like to make is that I understand that some time this month the department of Indian affairs is sending some senior officials to northwestern Ontario specifically to deal with those areas north of the lakehead. At this time I should like to request the minister to send those officials, if possible, to the Sioux Lookout, Red Lake, and Kenora areas where they will be able to see the pattern of Indian development in this part of northwestern Ontario. A great deal has to be done and a great deal can be done, particularly in the Red Lake area where there is a shortage of manpower for the gold mines in that vicinity. The Indians have been tried for this work and have demonstrated that they are satisfactory employees if provided with the necessary counselling services and housing accommodation. I think that this would be an invaluable experience for the minister's officials and it cannot help but improve the lot of the Indians in that area.

We have had something to say about this interesting bill on several occasions. It appears to be the standard form of incorporation but I believe a great departure has been made in two or three different ways. We are dealing with a life insurance company and I am of the opinion that there is absolutely no need for additional life insurance companies in Canada. This opinion, I may add, is shared by many of my hon. friends. Therefore I think we might reach a conclusion simply on the basis of whether or not Canadian interests would be served by the creation of another life insurance company which would do nothing more than is done by any other such company.
One of my hon. friends on the committee dealt with this point at some length. He is much opposed to the creation of any new life insurance companies for the simple reason that they would serve no purpose and in many cases they would even be detrimental to the economy. Obviously, if the business is spread around somebody in this field will starve to death. If there are enough insurance companies, their agents selling insurance will not be able to make a living.
There is another aspect which we must take into consideration before creating new life insurance companies. As I told a friend of mine not long ago, the activities of such companies are more detrimental to the Canadian economy than are those of the banks. Some of these companies probably have more assets to distribute than one of the smaller banks in Canada. The money collected by them does not just sit in the treasury. It continues to grow and the expansion of these funds is formidable. The result is that unless we are totally committed to the free enterprise system-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: UNITED INVESTMENT LIFE ASSURANCE COMPANY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: UNITED INVESTMENT LIFE ASSURANCE COMPANY

I can well appreciate that the hon. member would applaud in any case. The free enterprise system means to some that everyone is able to do everything he wishes to the detriment of himself and others. There must be some limitation upon the number of people engaged in a particular field or no one will be able to make a living from it. If belief in free enterprise means that everybody does the same thing, one is coming close to the communist philosophy.
This company, I understand, is not a normal life insurance company. It is being formed by an investment company which over a period of time has been selling mutual 
funds in a satisfactory way. At the present time United Accumulative Fund Limited which will own and operate this company possesses something like $300 million in assets. This makes it a sizeable enterprise, no matter how you look at it, not one of the shoestring type which believe they are going into the business to manufacture money as many of the promoters of small life insurance companies believe. This company has decided that while it is necessary for an individual to establish some sort of retirement fund for his future it is just as necessary for him to provide himself with short-term life insurance to cover the period in which his investments are not large enough to provide the result he wishes to achieve. It is said that on a short-term basis term insurance is the answer.
I am one of those who agree. I think it is safe to say that an insurance policy bought today will never produce the standard of living or the equivalent of the value of that policy at any other time in our history. Even the Minister of Finance would be hard put to answer if he were asked to say whether on a short-term basis $1,000 invested in an endowment policy today would ten years from now provide more money or less money or more purchasing power or less than the same amount at the time of investment.
[DOT] (6:10 p.m.)
People who bought $1,000 worth of insurance 20 or 30 years ago now find it has a purchasing value of only $400 or thereabouts. But the $1,000 that they invested originally formed a large part of their wages or other resources. In this respect this company has gone a long way toward solving a problem that has always concerned me, that of companies selling endowment plans without any stipulation to provide for escalation to meet increases in the cost of living. The federal government was not that foolish. When we passed the Canada Pension Plan we included an escalation clause to provide for increased cost of living. To my knowledge no insurance company does this, and this company in going into term insurance does not make such provision.
I have seen the figures and have been surprised at the amount of accumulated funds this company has in its mutual investment plan. There have been fantastic gains in the mutual field. Holdings in the mutual fund have increased substantially over the last 20 or 30 years. But if a person had invested in this mutual fund 30 years ago and died in the interim, his estate would not have received
July 4, 1967

Private Bills
the accumulated gains that otherwise would have been paid had he lived. I understand that under its mutual fund this company buys some 60 individual stocks and has been successful in protecting its investments, but it still sells term insurance to investors in the fund so that relief is provided investors' relatives if an investor suddenly dies.
This is a highly controversial field. I have received representations from insurance companies that are highly pleased about mutual funds being combined with an insurance company. I would agree with these representations if the insurance concerned was anything but term insurance. A mutual fund will rise and fall according to two principal factors. One is the business acumen behind it and the other is the fluctuation in the nation's gross national product.
Under the Ontario workmen's compensation plan 100 per cent disability compensation paid to a miner 30 years ago amounted to about $80 a month. Today that compensation is in the neighbourhood of $400 a month, but no provision is made to increase the amount according to the cost of living factor. Year after year the compensation board reports to the government without recommending any form of escalation with respect to the compensation paid.
Endowment policies issued by insurance companies do not take into account escalation in our standard of living. Term insurance protects only on a short-term basis. It is the type of insurance that a company takes out on a young executive, someone it hopes will make a contribution to the company. It is the type of insurance taken out on a partnership. In this respect the bill attracts my support. I am sure it will encourage other insurance companies to put escalation clauses in their policies.
There are other reasons which lead me to support the bill. One is the type of amendment that has been accepted by the company. It is in keeping with statements we heard last night when coming out of the N.D.P. convention which showed a growing interest on the part of many people in the necessity to have Canadian ownership and control of large corporations in Canada. This company has gone a long way toward satisfying the wish that I am sure all members of parliament have to see greater control of corporations fall into the hands of Canadians. The way it has done so is quite complicated and unique, but the company is to be highly commended for its effort to satisfy this aspiration of Canadians.
[DOT] (6:20 p.m.)
The people in this company with whom I have dealt are Canadians. They have agreed to accept the amendment. Although initially the money put up for this company will be almost 100 per cent American and will be supplied by a group called United Fund Management Limited, under the terms of the amendment after a period of 10 years voting control over the insurance company will fall into the hands of Canadian representatives. As I see it, it will mean that the control will remain with the Canadians who have bought stock in the company because the non-resident, be it a corporate entity or otherwise, will not be able to vote either by proxy or in person if the control is over 50 per cent.
I think this is a great step forward. I know there are many members on the other side who have not paid any attention to these insurance companies and in fact have paid no attention to private bills. It is my opinion, however, that some of the things which happen during private members' hours warrant a much greater degree of attention than they receive. I believe that the development and the future of Canada to a great extent are involved in many of the bills which are presented during private members' hours.
This company, being large and wealthy, apparently will be the kind of company in respect of whose operations we in Canada would like to have some say. We would also like to be assured that it will operate in the interests of Canada. In the main the sums of money which are accumulated by insurance companies are invested in the United States rather than in Canada. It is surprising that although many of these companies are Canadian their investment picture indicates that they are investing their money in the United States. Canada finds itself in the peculiar position of always having to have subsidiary companies enter the country. When they do so they bring in money which in many instances we have lent them from our own Canadian companies. They bring this money in to invest in our natural and other resources. At the same time we have no control or say in respect of their investment or the subsidiary nature of the operations.

Mr. Chairman, the closing remarks of the hon. member for Timiskaming have given me an opportunity to make some further observations with regard to the incorporation of this insurance investment company and many others like it. During the course of the past few years, both in the federal parliament and the provincial legislatures, it seems to me that during private members' hour or private members' day, whichever is applicable, there has been a tendency toward the passage of more and more bills of this kind.
I believe many members would agree that there has been a proliferation of financial institutions in this country. Some will say, of course, that as our economy has been growing and developing it is the normal order of things to have an increase in the number of financial institutions such as finance companies, trust and loan companies, investment companies and the like as a means to provide some support for the development of our national economy. Surely, however, there must be some point at which it can be said with accuracy that the number of such institutions has gone beyond the optimum point. This is my distinct impression and I gather from the remarks of my colleague, the hon. member for Timiskaming, that it is his impression as well.
I do not believe that at either the provincial or federal level in this country there has been a definitive study of the number of such institutions which would be desirable. I realize it would be very difficult to ascertain just what the optimum number should be, but it seems to me we should make some effort in this direction. Otherwise we will just carry on passing the necessary private members' bills to incorporate an ever growing number of such firms. In the general order of things, when it becomes clear in the business and financial community that there have been too many incorporations, a process of merger and amalgamation then takes place. This is all part of the wheeling and dealing of the business world. Some of this is to be expected and perhaps some of it is even to be welcomed, but surely some of it does result in gross inefficiencies and affects the economic structure of this country.
With specific reference to Bill No. C-114, during the committee hearings the superintendent of insurance was questioned fairly closely by certain hon. members concerning whether or not the subject matter of this legislation was acceptable and met all the standard requirements and forms. It is rather [The Assistant Deputy Chairman.]
interesting to read some of the evidence in this regard. We find in the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the committee on finance, trade and economic affairs that apparently the superintendent of insurance is of the opinion that it is a bit irregular to incorporate a life insurance company which will specialize in term insurance. It would seem that his opinion is that the record over the years has been a rather poor one in so far as specialized term insurance companies being able to maintain solvency is concerned. Yet in the end he offers the opinion that perhaps this company will survive or remain solvent, not because it is a specialized type of insurance company but rather in spite of that and because of the power of a rather large and well established parent company in the United States. I believe the name given here is Waddell and Reid.
I do not intend to say anything in connection with the relationship between the corporation seeking to be established here and the fact that it will specialize in term insurance. I wish, however, to make some reference to the fact that in the opinion of the superintendent of insurance this specialized insurance corporation can remain solvent because of its backing by a parent firm in the United States.
This leads me to make some reference to the foreign ownership and control aspect which is involved here. I think I must disagree a little with my colleague from Timiskaming when he offers the opinion that the amendment, which will be new clause 8 of the bill, will provide an adequate safeguard that the corporation to be established will ultimately come under Canadian ownership and control.
[DOT] (6:30 p.m.)
The effect of the amendment as I understand it is that the majority ownership will eventually come into Canadian hands, but that control of the company might not, because of the interconnection of the operating company, another holding company, and the corporation which would be established by this bill. While there may be even a large degree of Canadian ownership it seems very evident that the control will remain effectively in the hands of the operating firm and one of the intermediary holding companies for an indefinite period of time. That is how I understand clause 8. If I am wrong I would accept a correction.
A private member is really hard put to-determine just how he should react to and vote on a bill of this kind. It would seem on.
July 4. 1967

the one hand to be relatively innocuous or harmless to keep on incorporating an ever growing number of this kind of financial or insurance corporation. When one thinks about them one must conclude there is an optimum point beyond which we should not go in this proliferation. To go beyond that point would only serve to hurt the economy and increase the cost of essential production. They are not really the kind of organization that produces anything. They will eventually do nothing but increase the cost of providing a financial service.
In a way I was somewhat surprised that another financial concern should want to incorporate yet another life insurance company, particularly because of the reaction of life insurance companies to the recommendations of the Carter commission report. These companies were not in favour of being forced out of business, and their reaction to some of the recommendations of the commission report was so negative and reflected so much of the black side one would have thought we would never again see legislation through which groups of financiers were seeking to incorporate another insurance company. The reaction would indicate that these people felt it very unprofitable to implement the recommendations of this report.
I must also react somewhat negatively to one aspect of this bill because it appears that the people behind it are really seeking to use a specialized kind of term insurance as an ancillarly operation to their main operation of selling mutual funds, stocks or shares. It seems that this kind of operation is more of a promotional one, and one must wonder out loud whether this in itself is sufficient justification for granting incorporation through this bill.

Mr. Chairman, I have found a chart which indicates a point I was trying to make earlier. Before referring to it let me say that I believe the hon. member for Springfield is correct in his assessment of what this amendment does. The fact that Canadians may control 50 per cent of the stock of the company does not necessarily mean they control its operations. I know of some companies which have 90 per cent of their stock owned by Canadians, but their operations are not controlled by Canadians. I have heard it said that certain people who own only 3 per cent of the stock of a company control those companies. I do not know how they do this, or what is behind this type of phenomenon, but
Private Bills
I know it can happen. Let me give one example. United States control of the stock of the Bell Telephone Company of Canada is very small, but this company is in some way interrelated with the Bell company of the United States. That company has manufacturing companies which serve identical purposes. The United States company does control the Canadian company, and the influence of the United States company is much greater than would normally be the case in relation to its holdings.
I have not yet learned how this situation can occur but I am sure there are members in this house who do know. They certainly are not going to tell us because it would not be in their interest to do so. I was always of the opinion that if you owned 50 per cent of the stock of a company you could control it, but obviously this is not so. They tried to teach me at the university how this situation could occur but they were not very successful. Perhaps I should enrol again to find out, but I am not really sure that one could learn by taking an economics course.
The hon. member for Springfield is probably quite right in that this amendment does not go as far as he would like, but even he, with his greater knowledge in this field, must agree that it has gone a hell of a lot further than the original bill. It certainly goes a lot further toward what we want to accomplish than the next bill on the order paper.
I also agree with the hon. member for Springfield that it seems strange to amalgamate a term insurance company with a life insurance company, hard pressed as these life insurance companies are today. Let us not kid ourselves, they are spending a lot of money in attempting to incorporate about 20 or 30 companies each year. If they keep this up we will not refer to these companies by their names, but rather by number, and we will have to add the letters of the alphabet to that reference before long.
This chart I have, put out by United Investments and dated March 31, 1967, points out that the purchasing power of a dollar had dropped by 20 points from 1957 to 1967. It also showed that during the same period values on the Toronto Stock Exchange climbed 90 points.
[DOT] (6:40 p.m.)
So we see there has been an increase in stocks, and I presume there is a relationship-although I would not hazard a guess as to how you calculate it or what it is-in the gross national product of our country and,

July 4, 1967

although perhaps even more remote, in our standard of living. The Toronto stock market figures indicate that this has gone up to 90. In March, 1967, this company went up to 160 points. It seems to me, therefore, that if the standard of living in any degree follows the increase in the Toronto stock market, namely to 90, the fact that this company has gone to 160 proves that it has been a relatively good investment. Also the purchasing power of the dollar going 20 points the other way has not been a good thing.
It is very interesting to study some of the tables put out by the company. The table I have in my hand deals with mutual investment funds over an eight year period to December 31, 1965. If you invested $10,000 in 1957, by 1965 you would have accumulated $26,700. I think this would be a fairly good type of insurance policy. It means that at the end of this period you would have accumulated almost three times as much as you had invested. I believe this is not unreasonable when compared with the increase in our standard of living.
This table also indicates that if you had invested your money in a trust company at 4J per cent, by 1965 your investment would have increased in value tremendously. If you had invested $4,200 at 9 per cent interest-I suppose the 9 per cent applies to the mortgage and insurance field-at the end of the period your investment would be worth $20,000. Some very interesting conclusions can be drawn from the figures contained in this table. I must confess that I do not understand some aspects of the matter. However, if one had been born near the time of confederation, the table indicates that if you had invested $100 in 1871, by 1961 that investment would have been worth $325,000, and now it would be worth $360,890. I suppose this shows that our grandparents did not put their money in the right place.
I am not necessarily a proponent of mutual funds, but if the stock market, the standard of living and the cost of living continue to bear a relationship there is really no point in buying insurance. I have an endowment policy with an insurance company, so I know what I am talking about. You are as lucky as hell if you get your money back at the end of 20 years. The only way you can really win is by dying in the first year of the policy. If you die at any time later than this you have made a poor investment. I should have put my money into mutual funds some time ago, rather than into insurance. It seems to me that term insurance is for a person who wants

to take a gamble on the cost of living, the standard of living and increases in the stock market. He would be able to gamble in this respect with short term investment.
There are charts here that I do not understand. Mr. Humphrys should explain some of them to us because I do not understand them all. For this reason perhaps I should not quote them, because we will all become confused. I quote from a table dealing with a yearly insurance premium of $45 invested at 9 per cent. This gives you the figure of $114 and a yearly cost of $160. It would give you, if you died at 35 years of age during the initial year, $10,000. Your accumulated value of the investment would be $125. Your total benefit realized on death at 35 years of age in the first year of the policy would be $10,125. The table goes on to show that at age 64 you would have $525 worth of insurance but you would have a total asset of $17,569. From then on you would pay no more money on the term insurance, but by the time you reached 75-if any of us are that lucky-you would have $43,982 to leave to your heirs, I presume, because most of us find you can't take it with you.
For these reasons this type of insurance policy lends itself to a great deal of consideration. The day should be here when every hon. member who has insurance is taking a look at that insurance. Since becoming interested in these companies I have realized that I have never been a financial success, because I bought this type of life insurance, which has no value. It has certainly been a damned poor investment. Unless I had died in the first year of the policy the investment is not really worth while. It is too late now to do anything about that, and I will be lucky to get my money back at the end of the insurance period. If the value of the dollar keeps going down I will not get a quarter of my money back. They have taken 75 per cent of my investment and I shall not benefit from it unless we have another depression; and none of us wants that.
Those members who are really serious about the proliferation of insurance companies will have to consider carefully this aspect of the matter in terms of what people are getting out of the insurance companies and how they are to get their money back. I do not mean how they are to get their money back in terms of dollars, because I am sure that if you buy an insurance policy worth $1,000 you will get $1,000 back, in terms of dollars. But if the dollar is worth only 50
July 4, 1967

cents you will not get back $1,000 in purchasing power but only $500. If the value of the dollar drops lower than 50 cents, you will get even less back, although in terms of actual dollars you will obviously get them back.
I do not know of any member of parliament who stood up in this house and opposed the escalation clause in the Canada Pension Plan. But this is really what we are talking about. Whatever money is invested by an individual, we want him to have the kind of retirement that the money would buy when invested. If you look over the history of the last 20 years you see that the insurance dollar is worth only about one third its original value by the time a person retires. The escalation clause in the Canada Pension Plan will prevent this situation developing.
I do not know whether the sponsor of the bill wishes to explain the other point raised. It is my understanding that the amendment will provide Canadian ownership, to a degree, over a period of time.
