speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the minister about the work that is being carried out by the Company of Young Canadians in the areas of the north. How many ventures or how many projects have they undertaken? I am asking these questions because of the many rumours suggesting that this group leaves a great deal to be desired. I am dealing with the matter now because this is one of the fields in which the Prime Minister felt the Company of Young Canadians would be very active and useful. I am a little bit disturbed because I have a report here which would indicate that perhaps they are not as useful as the Prime Minister thought they would be. The report reads:
[DOT]-an unkempt collection of youthful layabouts held a five day meeting. The 69 members who

turned up for some or all of the sessions spent $4,738 on transportation alone; $226 on telephone calls and $3,930 on food and accommodation. All this produced not so much as a single report; the parliamentary secretary to the Prime Minister advised the house that none could be expected, although he believed a member of the staff had made some record of the sessions.
Now, Mr. Chairman, that is a very disturbing statement. I raise the matter also because of the cost. There are only 66 volunteers in this Company of Young Canadians, and that is 2,440 short of the number the Prime Minister expected. In spite of this, the estimates covering this group have gone up to $2,445,000. This is the amount that will be provided in the next year. I believe these questions deserve answers. What have they done in this department of young Canadians in comparison with the accomplishments the Prime Minister expected? Their figures break down to about $37,000 per volunteer, or about equal to a tax of 12 cents on every man, woman and child in Canada. This is not very good for a government that finds itself, in boom times, with one of the largest deficits ever faced in the history of Canada. This deficit situation is constantly eroding the fixed income and pensions of those who have retired. It is also increasing the cost of living, and now we have the highest cost of living in this country of all time, coupled with the highest taxes.
Perhaps there are other instances, Mr. Chairman, in which this company did not perform very well. Since we are considering the estimates of the Indian affairs branch, I should like to know just what functions this group performed and what the Canadian taxpayer is going to get for his $2,444,800. I should like to know also how many Indian hospitals are operating today, and how many are operated by the Indian affairs branch? Has there been a decrease? How many have been taken over by the provinces or municipalities? I should like to know, too, how many doctors are now employed by the Indian affairs branch and how great has been the decrease, if any, over the last few years?
Then, Mr. Chairman, I should like to know how many of these doctors operate under medicare plans, that is when they are outside of the Northwest Territories or in the provinces. Does the provincial hospital commission check the regulations of the hospitals under the Indian affairs branch.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
I am also very interested in the government's educational program. Out of a total budget of $100 million, as the minister says we
July 4, 1967

are spending $47 million on education. Integration into the educational system is proceeding quickly. This is all to the good if the end results are proving fruitful. Indian children are attending school in my home town and are doing very well. I think it is very worth while to integrate Indian children with white school children in our town schools, with all the advantages of the generally superior facilities in those town schools.
I should like to know from the minister how many children are attending the primary and secondary schools. I also want to know the method of payment involved. Perhaps I should know the answer, but I do not know whether a per capita tax basis is used or not. I should also like to ask the minister whether any Indian reserves have been sold outright or abandoned, how many have been put on a long term lease and what properties have been leased across Canada by Indian reserves. I ask the minister what part his department has played in these negotiations. Does some body or company who wants to develop the area deal with the Indians directly and, if so, what part does the department play in those negotiations? It is important to see to it that any deals that are made are equitable and the money properly invested in securities.
I should also like to ask the minister whether the department has made an assessment of how many Indian reserves on islands are close enough to the mainland for it to be practical economically to build a bridge or causeway to the mainland. I have spoken to the minister about this matter before, and I should like to give him a case in point. I have in mind Christian island, which is a mile and a half across from the mainland. The deepest point in the channel is approximately 17 feet. This island is about seven miles long. Many school children come across to the mainland to attend secondary school at Midland and Penetang', and they cross by boat. In the stormy part of the year and when the lake is frozen over it is difficult to get across for about a month. Not only that, Mr. Chairman, but often they have to stand on the wharf and wait for the boat morning and night, and it can be pretty cold.
Has the department looked into the economic aspects of this situation? I expect the costs would be shared, because the provincial government has already installed hydro and there is a radio telephone system on the island. Many properties on the island have been rented, but the only transportation to the mainland is by the boat Hooey. As the number of cottages on the island increases the
Supply-Indian Affairs situation worsens, and on many occasions the boat is loaded and people wait on week ends. Roads are being built on the island so there will be cars taken across. These cars have to be ferried across by scow.
At this point I should like to congratulate the minister on being someone you can talk to, who will listen to your argument or the point you are raising with him. The minister pays the most careful attention and I congratulate him on this. I realize he has a big department to manage. I also know that ten years ago the provincial government and federal government both said that in another ten years a bridge or causeway to Christian island would be feasible economically. Boom times have been prevailing ever since, so I should like to know what both these governments have in mind in this regard and particularly this government, as they have the administration of the island.
I should like to explore this matter a little further by asking the minister to look into the economics of the situation. What does it cost to keep this boat in service and to keep it manned? What is the cost of maintaining the facilities at Cedar Point? For years a new dock had to be constructed every second year or so, as the minister will discover on looking over past estimates, but about seven to eight years ago the government headed by the present Leader of the Opposition constructed a dock with a proper breakwater which has proved to be trouble free. I should like to know what could be gained by building a causeway and opening up the island in that way. As I say, houses on the island are being rented so some sort of policy must have been set. If we are going to continue to use the present dock, let us utilize it to the full, which may mean additional costs in facilities.
I realize that the minister will have to consult with the provincial government before he can give me an answer, but if he follows his general practice I will hear from him during the next month whether this project is economically feasible. As I say, I have raised the matter before and both houses indicated ten years ago that such a project would be feasible in ten years time. In the meantime there has been great growth and I should like to know whether they feel this project can now go ahead.
If it is proceeded with it would be of great advantage to the Indian children. They would get to school more easily. At the moment the buses wait at Cedar Point, being parked out

July 4, 1967
Supply-Indian Affairs at night and having to start cold in the mornings. These Indian children do not find it easy to reach school and I know that the minister would like to help them in whatever way he can.
The minister has mentioned integration of Indian children, which I am sure is a wonderful idea. However, I was a little puzzled by a report I saw in a Toronto newspaper one day which indicated there might be 15,000 Indians in that city who were experiencing difficulties. They were not being assimilated into the community, but sticking together in their own groups. Just last week an Indian girl was strangled to death in a certain part of the red light district in Toronto-that is, if they have a red light district; I do not know whether they admit to that or not. But if it is true there are 15,000 Indians in Toronto many of whom are not being assimilated and looked after properly, then what is to be gained by taking these Indians from their reserves and placing them in a society in which they do not mesh?
I should like to know what the minister has to say on this score because I think it raises a very important point. It is not good enough to take Indians off the reserves or encourage them and send them to our big cities where we let them disintegrate morally and socially. I cannot vouch personally for the truth of this story, but it was in the press and perhaps the minister read it, and generally when there is smoke there is fire.
I should like to dwell for a few moments on the restoration of Cahiague in my area which is situated in the neighbourhood of Warminster. The minister has been very sympathetic to this project, but I understand that it is not going ahead very quickly this summer. A lot of work has been done by Professor Emerson in the past. The northern end at Martyrs Shrine has been developed and hundreds of thousands of dollars spent. I was there last Saturday and saw that the whole Indian village has been restored. Yet I am told that Cahiague in former times was a bigger Indian city-if they called them cities-than Fort Ste-Marie.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
I am all in favour of what has been done at the shrine. I wish to congratulate all parties concerned, including the provincial government and the federal government which did play a part in this restoration-the Department of Public Works dredged the river and gave other help. However, I suggest the minister should consider once again the position
(Mr. Rynard.]
of some of these historic sites and ask himself whether we should not be doing something more than is being done at present. The hon. gentleman has probably studied this question and is as well aware of these things as I am. He knows that this area is rich in historic value-rich in the spiritual values of yesterday. The Jesuit priests came to this area-Father Caron was among those who came up with Champlain-and it was here that every one of those Jesuits that followed him paid the supreme sacrifice for their Christian ideals. It was to Christian island that these people fled-I think there were only 29 of them left after the Iroquois attacked and slaughtered most of them. I should like to see further attention paid to this site because I feel our efforts are probably lagging behind here.
In closing, let me say I realise there are differences of opinion with regard to the way in which Indian affairs should be handled. It is true one can take Indians from the reserves and settle them in the big cities. But what is the use of doing this if we-and they-lose sight of the very reasons for which they were moved into the cities.
In conclusion, I should like the minister to turn his attention to the matters I have brought up. He has always done so in the past and I hope for an answer from him either this evening or in the near future.

I simply wish to record in Hansard a very special event which took place last Friday, June 30-the presentation of a piece of true Indian pottery by Mrs. Oliver Smith of the Six Nations Indian Reserve at Ohsweken in the County of Brant to Her Majesty the Queen of Canada. In return, Mrs. Smith was of course received by Her Majesty. What greater honour could anyone, any nation, receive?
We who know these true Canadians and live near them are greatly honoured and privileged to have such a lovely lady as Mrs. Smith, who comes from the historic Six Nations Reserve, represent us on such occasions.
I should like to add a piece of information, which possibly few members have heard. Mrs. Smith, who represented us in presenting this piece of pottery, is none other than a sister of Tonto, that great television star. Might I also add that her very lovely daughter, an educated daughter who has taught school, won the Miss Ontario beauty contest a few years ago.

speechtext:
Hear, hear.
July 4, 1967

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the Indians of the Six Nations form one of our most progressive groups of true Canadians in educational and cultural matters. We call to mind such names as the Andersons-incidentally, the present chief is an Anderson-the Jamiesons, the Montagues, the Montures, the Kings, the Moses, the Hills and many others. Last, but not least, we think of the Longboats and of that great distance runner Tom Longboat who made a name not only for his nation but for Canada.
A few moments ago I said the Six Nations represent advancement. Let me add that they do not forget the past-and it is most important that no nation, no people, should forget the past, because if they do they have no guide by which to enter the future. They produce a pageant every autumn, acting out the history of their nation and of Indian life in a natural setting of water and trees. Hundreds of people attend this colourful program each year, leaving with increased knowledge of the Indian people and their ways. But to me, and I am sure to the Indians, most important of all is the fact that in performing this pageant they are keeping before their children, and future generations of their people, the wonder of their ancient history and culture. May it last for ever.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
I should like to raise a point which I believe has been brought up annually for some years-I recall my hon. friend from Cariboo drawing attention to it last year. I refer to the tax imposed on those who have to enter national parks for business purposes, not intending to spend time in the park, as a park.
A toll station has been set up on the trans-Canada highway in British Columbia and a toll is charged, ostensibly for admission to the park. Admittedly one payment is good for entering all the national parks in Canada for the rest of the year in which it is made. However, this is not of much use to a member of the public whose travel in a national park has been undertaken for purposes not at all concerned with the park itself, and who would not be visiting any of the other national parks during the course of the year.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
It seems to me there is an injustice here and a principle that is being violated. There is taxation of a section of the population with nothing given in return. The problem has been heightened by the fact that the commission on redistribution, in a complete lapse of
Supply-Indian Affairs good sense or reason, put together my constituency and that of Kootenay East to make a new hybrid called Okanagan-Kootenay. The main bodies of population lie at opposite ends of the new constituency. The meeting point for these two groups of people must be half way between them, and that makes it the town of Golden.
All of the political parties in the area are in the course of reorganizing constituency organizations. This means that during any given year hundreds of people from all the varied political parties-and they are all represented in that region-will make the trip to Golden for purposes that have nothing to do with the national park through which they travel. Yet they will have to pay the toll, and coming as they do from the park-like beauty of the Okanagan it is quite possible they would not feel the urge to visit any other national parks.
I wonder what is the revenue obtained through this means and whether it is not within the capability of the department, so ably served by the minister, to come up with some solution that would separate park visitors from people just using the trans-Canada highway. In our literature on the trans-Canada highway we boast that it is toll free, but at that point in British Columbia it is not. This fee becomes for many people a toll to use the trans-Canada highway and not a toll to visit the national parks of Canada. I submit that legitimate park visitors should be separated from people who have to travel this route by necessity, or else the tax should be applied evenly across the country, whereby $2 would be collected from all automobile users and applied to the upkeep of the national parks. I think some equitable system could be worked out by which this toll could be removed from people who have to use that highway for purposes other than visiting this national park.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Before dealing specifically with Indian affairs, Mr. Chairman, I would like to say I think the minister should be commended for what appears to be a much more realistic and reasonable approach to the whole problem of Indian affairs than we have witnessed for a good many years. From the numerous press releases and circulars that cross my desk, it seems to me the minister is very interested in his department and is trying to do a good job with the means available to him. I have just one question I would like him to answer later, and it concerns the integration project at Elliot Lake.

July 4, 1967
Supply-Indian Affairs
It was decided to open up about 20 of the abandoned houses at Elliot Lake and move some 20 Indian families from 200 miles north of Sioux Lookout into them. I understand the men of the families were given $15 a day to cover expenses for themselves and their families while they were sent to the school of continuing education at Elliot Lake, in order to gain technical and vocational training of some sort. I am not sure how far this project has moved along and I would be very interested to know whether it is meeting with success, because I understand it is one of the first attempts to integrate Indian and white populations.
There is one Indian reserve in my riding. I spent some time there and was astounded to find that only about half of the homes on the reserve were being occupied. I am speaking of the Mattagami Indian reserve, about 24 miles north of the Canadian National main line. The Indians told me one of the reasons they were moving out of the reserve was lack of facilities, particularly lack of a decent road to get into and out of the reserve.
There was a serious problem in the winter months if anyone on the reserve got sick. I believe at one time the provincial department of lands and forests kept a road clear during the winter months, but then its efforts slackened. In fact it stopped plowing the road for a time, and the only way the Indians could reach outer civilization was by snowshoeing out to the village. However, an arrangement was made between the Indian agent and the provincial department of lands and forests as a result of which the department agreed to keep the road cleared. But this is not an easy proposition, and in times of bad storm it is not unusual for this little community to be isolated for two or three days.
When there I also inquired about the financial status of the Indians. Those best off made around $1,200 a year, and over all their annual earnings varied between $600 and $1,200 a year. Naturally they were having a difficult time getting by. It is an area where groceries and other things fetch high prices.
At one time it was a good trapping area, but as most hon. members know, trapping today is not a very profitable enterprise. As a result these Indians are in a precarious position, particularly during the winter months. Their houses, in effect only shells, are in a deplorable condition.
Some of the Indians have moved into the nearby village, where they have obtained employment, are doing reasonably well, and

have integrated to a reasonable extent with the white population. I inquired what they thought was the best solution to their problem. They said they felt they were being discriminated against, and felt that employment could be found for them in their natural environment up in the north woods. They were a little dismayed that the provincial department of lands and forests were using students, and what I believe are called junior rangers, during the summer months to clear out parkland, of which there is a considerable acreage in the area. They felt this was an area where they could definitely do just as good or a better job. They also believed it would help them solve the financial problems. I realize this is a matter which would have to be worked out in conjunction with the provincial government, but I believe it is something worth looking into.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
My colleague, the hon. member for Springfield, mentioned the matter of guiding. Any of us who come from the northern part of any province realize that guiding can be a quite profitable means of employment. I believe it is regrettable that something is not done to ensure that any party going into the woods must be accompanied by a guide. Here again I understand that this is something which has to come under the jurisdiction of the provinces. I think, however, it should be pointed out that any party which goes out with an Indian as a guide does not leave a forest fire behind when leaving the woods. I think this also is something well worth considering.
I was quite interested to read a press release in the Toronto Globe and Mail dated February 20, 1967, wherein it is reported that the minister stated that 215,000 reserve Indians would be given their emancipation, as he put it, under new legislation which would be brought out by his department. I am wondering how this is progressing and whether it is feasible.
I believe it was the hon. member for Peace River who made a statement with which I agree very much. He said that you cannot adopt an over-all policy for Indians in general, but that each area must be dealt with on the basis of what is required in that particular area. I believe this is quite evident. I have received correspondence from Indians in various parts of Ontario and of British Columbia, and it would seem to me that the problems in one area do not apply in so far as another area is concerned. What we must
July 4, 1967

realize more than anything else, I believe, is that it is necessary to place ourselves in the position of the Indian, so that we will understand his thinking. After all he is being subjected to our rules and regulations with very little say in regard to how they affect his destiny.
I believe the minister's idea of giving self rule to the Indians, if it can be carried out effectively-and I realize this cannot be done overnight-would be one of the biggest steps forward, because I think it is the only way the Indians will eventually integrate with the white population and become self sufficient citizens.
Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to take up very much more time. In passing I should like to say I was quite impressed by the remarks made by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River prior to the supper recess. Having been in that area I realize the great problem there. I should like to commend him for his very forthright statements in connection with the problems, and also for the comments he made with regard to the manner in which he thinks these problems should be handled.

Mr. Chairman, I promise to be very brief. I should just like the minister to clear up something concerning which I attempted to obtain an answer the other day. During his term of office has he taken any initiative in the development of a national park in Ontario. Surely he must realize there is a great need for a national park development in this province. We have here a concentration of industrial workers who in ever increasing numbers will be in need of much more recreational and park accommodation in the years ahead.
Does not the minister think that no time should be lost in acquiring and preserving for posterity some of our Ontario wilderness areas, which are disappearing at a rapid rate. In these areas our many species of wildlife might have a haven suitable for their continued reproduction. A sizeable national park in Ontario would bring big dividends for time unlimited.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, perhaps the debate at this time on Indian affairs at least, which is the subject matter in which I have a stronger interest than some others which come under the minister's jurisdiction, may be rather futile and simply a bit of an exercise. I say "futile" in the sense that such a debate may have little opportunity to influence government policy which, I believe, is
Supply-Indian Affairs the prime purpose of debate. It also may provide little opportunity for public expression of some of the feelings which the native Indian people have about their own destiny and the activities of the government.
One of the matters which has interfered with an opportunity to go fully into the matter of Indian affairs in any great depth has been that of time. If we harken back just a few years I believe we will see that over the last three fiscal years, including this one, there has not yet been an opportunity, at least that was realized, to go with any great detail into the matter of Indian affairs and government policy. In 1965 there was not much opportunity for debate, because that was the year in which we had a summer recess of parliament, with the promise that the estimates would be considered in the fall of that year. Instead of having the estimates we had an election, which interfered with any orderly consideration of matters in parliament.
The estimates in respect of the expenditures for 1965 really were considered retroactively, or after the expenditures had been made and at a time when we were in a new session to concern ourselves with the spending program for 1966. During the last session the estimates of the Indian affairs branch were referred to a committee. That committee made what I considered to be an extremely wise decision. It expressed the hope and desire that very soon the members of the committee would have an opportunity to visit Indian communities and the Indian people in order to examine at first hand as much as they possibly could the situation in the Indian communities, and in order to have an opportunity to speak intimately with the native people with regard to their feelings concerning Indian affairs.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
We have gone over this ground before, but I want to mention only briefly in passing that for one reason or another the committee found itself frustrated in its desire to carry out what is conceived to be a legitimate undertaking. The first thing that happened was that the committee decided it would be advantageous to break up into subcommittees, allowing easier handling of the situation and more visits to more communities. Accordingly a report was made to the house, but somewhere along the line there was a substitution by government in respect of committee authority, disallowing the subcommittees.

July 4. 1967
Supply-Indian Affairs
Last year in the fall, when the committee finally got around to meeting, tentative arrangements to visit a number of Indian communities were made. One community was in Quebec and the others were in the southern part of Ontario. It was found then that an insufficient number of members expressed a desire to make the visit. Consequently they could not be made because of a lack of quorum, and they were cancelled.
This cancellation caused a tremendous amount of ill feeling on the part of the native people in the communities to be visited because the advance arrangements which had been made were cancelled. The committee then came back to the house and asked again for authority to divide into subcommittees. This authority was forthcoming and the subcommittees did visit the Indian communities of Caughnawaga and St. Regis. I might add that prior to this, members of the committee had travelled to meet with the provincial advisory council, or board, of Ontario. Subsequent to the visit to Caughnawaga the committee laid out a tour of some of the communities of British Columbia, but this trip was cancelled. I might add that in conjunction with the British Columbia trip it was planned that some of the committee members en route to British Columbia would take the opportunity of stopping in Winnipeg to hold a watching brief in an Indian-Metis conference there.
These proposed trips were beset by obstacles, and the end of the session arrived. Because the committee early in the session last year conceived the idea of making visits to Indian communities in order to obtain an assessment of Indian affairs, it was decided to give only a scant or cursory examination of the estimates. Accordingly it reported the estimates to the house, where they were considered very briefly. Last session a time factor militated against any examination in depth of Indian affairs. During this session we are faced with the rules which impinge upon our consideration of these estimates. I am not complaining about these rules as they were agreed to by the house; nor am I trying to be objectionable in what I am saying. I am trying to make what I consider to be a factual statement, indicating that during this and the past two fiscal years there has been no opportunity to go into a detailed examination of Indian affairs.
To that extent I suggest that we may well be indulging in a futile exercise in attempting to influence government policy in respect of Indian affairs. That should be the purpose of

our debate; that is, to put across a point of view in the hopes that it will be accepted. It may well be that we are engaging in an exercise of futility because at least a part of the debate in parliament should reflect public thinking. I am rather inclined to think that this parliament is behind the times in trying to reflect the thinking and feelings of our native people in relation to government policy.
The minister in his opening remarks on June 9 pointed out that perhaps the salvation of the Indian people rested in the hands of those of the younger generation, and I think he made mention of the age of 26 years. It is true the wealth and progress of any group rests in the hands of youth because our future leaders come from that group. The younger people among the native population are of a different sort than their parents or elders. The older Indian people were more gentle, trusting and more resigned to accept their lot and position. Speaking in general terms, the older Indians expressed their dislike for government policy by ignoring it. In other words, instead of attending meetings for the purpose of discussing certain matters which might influence their position they avoided them. They showed their objection by non-participation.
As I say, younger people have a different concept and philosophy. They have been struck by the situation which exists in societies outside the Indian community. As a result of education and participation in the armed forces during the second world war, coupled with greater mobility, these young people have been able to travel, even with their limited resources and incomes, and have found out what is the situation in society outside the reservations. They want to know why there is this difference, and the answers they receive are not satisfactory. These people are very dissatisfied because of this new knowledge, coupled with their understanding of the history over the past decade of deceit on the part of non-Indian explorers and governments. I am sure the minister will not disagree that in years past there has been a great deal of mishandling of the rights of Indian people. Because of this history and the knowledge that they have been unfairly treated at the hands of non-Indians our Indian communities are becoming discontent. As a result they may take stronger action than we would like to see.
We must recognize that forces of discontent exist in these Indian communities, and these
July 4, 1967



people are beginning to discuss how they can use their strength to gain what they consider to be just and right.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
Practically every day in the past few years they and we have been able to read about the civil rights movement in the United States, which is a movement on behalf of a group of people who are distinct because they have skin of a different colour from ours. The native Indian has an affinity with them in that regard and in regard to the matter of fundamental rights. I hope we can overcome the combination of these two forces by exhibiting conscientiously and deliberately in every program of the government, by example and precept, the fact that government, government forces, parliament and the non-Indian community has respect for the native Indian people as a group and as individuals. I hope we can exhibit attitudes that will beget trust on the part of the Indian people toward government policies. I hope we can convince them that we will honour all the dealings that take place with their peoples.
It is no good engendering this trust in just one, two or a dozen instances. It must be a persistent, deliberate, conscious policy carried out at all levels of government and in all dealings that government has with our native people. It will take a period of time to overcome the inheritance the Indian people have in so far as their dealings at the hands of government and non-Indians are concerned.
Mr. Chairman, I might mention a few things in this regard to indicate, at least in so far as an assessment of this matter by the native people is concerned, where there is or has been a lack of openness and trustworthy dealings. Some time ago when the minister's predecessor was in office he announced the formation of an interdepartmental committee to deal with hunting, fishing and game rights of the native people. This was the result of persistent questioning in the house by members following the decisions made in connection with the Migratory Birds Convention Act, and a few other court cases of that sort.
When the announcement was made about the establishment of this committee the general understanding of the native Indian people was that the committee would be able to come up with some recommendations and suggestions as to what should be done. The minister at one stage when I inquired into this matter said the policy of the government was to let the courts-I am paraphrasing what he said-delineate the areas of dispute;
Supply-Indian Affairs in other words, let the courts make the decisions for or against the native people on hunting and fishing rights in respect of whatever instances were brought before the courts. This supposedly would give some guide line to government, which could then act upon the decisions made by the courts. The government could then see what legal impediments might exist in the way of doing something to cope with the disgruntlement of the native Indian people over loss of their hunting and fishing rights.
It is the minister's responsibility and duty, if he feels it is in the public interest, or for some other reason, not to make public that report of the interdepartmental committee, even though the minister said a precis of the report would be prepared and made available to all hon. members. I have been away from the house for the past week, but I do not think it has yet been prepared. In any event, this is the sequence of events: First, there was the announcement that this matter would be dealt with by an interdepartmental committee; then there was the announcement that the report of the interdepartmental committee would not be made public, and then the declaration that the courts would make decisions that would lay out the areas where disagreement might exist. This has all built up in the minds of a number of native Indian people with whom I have spoken and who have been watching this matter with some interest the understanding that once again government has not been true and faithful to them.
I am not saying that this is in fact the thought in the mind of the minister. I am sure it is not. But I tell him this is the thought in the minds of a number of native Indian people. This is what should be paramount and what should motivate our efforts in doing all we can to assist native Indian people. We must exhibit to them the full degree of respect that is necessary and show them that we are trustworthy in our dealings. That is just one example, Mr. Chairman.
Another example involves my own province of British Columbia. There not too long ago the minister of municipal affairs, Mr. Campbell, announced that the provincial government was desirous that Indian reserves should become municipalities, and he hoped that one of the Indian communities in his constituency of Campbell River would become the first Indian community to become a municipality. This on the surface may sound good, but in fact in so far as British Columbia is concerned it could very well mean that any Indian band which decided to

July 4. 1967
Supply-Indian Affairs become a municipality would lose every inch of its reserve land. None of them want to do this.
A few years ago there was a move by the Metlakatla people, near Prince Rupert-this was 15 or 20 years ago-to become a municipal structure under the laws of British Columbia. I ask the committee to remember that the Metlakatla people still feel the influence of Mr. Duncan, a missionary who was sometimes rather brutal and cruel in his dealings with native people but none the less had an influence upon them which exists in large measure today both amongst the people in Metlakatla, British Columbia, and their brothers and cousins in Metlakatla, Alaska. They desired to become a municipality. One of the difficulties that arose was that if those people became a municipality they would become enfranchised as a band under the Indian Act; in other words, they would lose as a band, and each individual in it, status as an Indian within the meaning of the Indian Act.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
The minute that came to pass, the provisions of an order in council passed by the provincial government would come into play. This is the damaging part. I should like to make reference to order in council 1036 made July 29, 1938. It is still in existence. The members of the executive council in attendance at that cabinet meeting and who made this order in council were Mr. Hart, Mr. Weir, Mr. Wismer, Mr. MacPherson, Mr. MacDonald and Mr. Pearson. That is not our Prime Minister but a gentleman who used to be the minister of labour of British Columbia. This was at a time when a Liberal government was in office in British Columbia under Hon. John Hart. This order in council relates to the land question in British Columbia, which still has not been solved. It points out that certain lands set out in the schedule to the Indian affairs settlements act-and the lands are the reserves which were set up at that time and which still exist except those parts which have been sold or surrendered-would be conveyed to the federal government to be held in trust for the native people. This was subject to condition, and the important part is that this is made subject to the condition that in the event of any Indian tribe or band in British Columbia at some future time becoming extinct, any lands hereby conveyed for such tribe or band and not sold or disposed of as heretofore provided, or any unexpended fund being the proceeds of any such sale, shall be conveyed or repaid to the grantor. In

other words, if an Indian band-and let us remember that the word "band" is legally defined in the Indian Act, and not a hereditary concept of a political or social unit of Indian people-becomes extinct, the reserve lands which it held previously revert to the provincial government. The two lawyers with whom I have discussed this matter, one of whom is very learned and knowledgeable in the field of Indian affairs and land titles, are of the opinion that if an Indian band becomes enfranchized, it then becomes extinct as an entity under the Indian Act and its reserve lands go back to the province. This was the barrier that prevented the people in Metlakatla some 15 years ago from becoming a municipality, the barrier being that the provincial government in Victoria, when Mr. Bob Sommers was the minister of lands and forests, refused to give up its authority, which it relegated to itself under this order in council, and refused to give up its rights to the reserve lands. So the Metlakatla people, who were desirous of becoming a political unit in British Columbia, found that if they decided to make any progress whatever in their political structure they would lose their reserve lands.
I submit that the same situation exists today. When Mr. Campbell, our minister of municipal affairs, starts speaking about the desirability of the Indian bands in British Columbia becoming municipalities, the native Indian people who know of this order in council and who have concerned themselves about the land problem in British Columbia for more years than I have been alive, say to themselves "You are not speaking with a straight tongue, Mr. Campbell, because you are asking us to become municipalities, and if we do so, the land that we now hold as reserve land will end up in the hands of the provincial government, plus the money from the proceeds of the sale of that land."
This is another example of the type of government pronouncements which are not backed by an honest and faithful declaration, which makes the Indian people sceptical of government dealings. The British Columbia Indian reserves minerals resources act, an agreement entered into by the government of Canada and the province of British Columbia in 1943, and endorsed by a statute of this parliament, is another example of bad faith on the part of governments. That act still exists on the statute books.
I gave two or three examples to point out that not only must the government declare, as the minister has done on a number of
July 4, 1967

occasions, that it is the government's intention to act honourably and faithfully and to develop a trustworthy relationship between the Indian people and the government of Canada, but must support such a declaration by action. Where this is not so, words become futile and will not have the beneficial influence that they should have in developing a decent rapport between the government and the Indian community.
There are many other items with which I could deal if I had the time to do so. I will only say that this is the third year in a row when parliament has not had the time to examine Indian affairs in any depth and to engage in a debate by an examination of the department, by making proposals and hearing the minister's comments and views regarding the merit of any proposal. My understanding of what parliament is doing with respect to the estimates of this year, is that we have three quarters of an hour left in this session to deal with the estimates of the department.
The committee on human rights and Indian affairs, which it was hoped last year would have some really worth while work to do, has not even been called together in this session. There was no effort made on the part of those who may have been nominated for office to call the committee to consider what we might do. It is too late now. This part of the session is almost at an end and we will have to wait until September or October before the committee can be called together.
May I say again in closing that there are too many examples of untrustworthy and unfair decisions which do not jibe with the laudatory statements made by the government concerning the work done in this field, and unless the two are put together we will not get too far in promoting and advancing the cause of our native Indian people. In fact that task may well be taken out of our hands by the native people themselves, because at the present time their mood is one of rebelliousness.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, tonight I should like to bring a point to the attention of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development which I brought up in the last session but with no positive results whatever. However I wish now to repeat, and I am sure the people of my consituency expect me to repeat and to keep on repeating, the plea that I am about to make. I refer to what I may call a deficiency or insufficiency of parks in my area in western Nova Scotia. I know that hundreds of thousands of Canadians and
Supply-Indian Affairs Americans know of our famous Cape Breton Highlands national park. The spectacular scenery and the breathtaking beauty of that park is renowned. I can safely say, moreover, that it has been a self-liquidating concern.
Tourism in Nova Scotia is second only to the fisheries in importance. And certainly the Cape Breton Highlands park has aided and fomented the tourist business. The Cape Breton national park is in the extreme north east of the province. Until a few years ago there was no park whatever in the western part of the province, where tourism plays a significant part in our economy; but about four years ago the government laudably decided to establish what was first known as the Western Nova Scotia national park. However, the fact that it does not extend into the west end of Nova Scotia may be one of the reasons why it is now called the Kejimkujik national park. Contiguous to the Kejimkujik park, which is located more in the central part of Nova Scotia than in western Nova Scotia, is an area known as the Tobeatic game sanctuary which is on provincial crown land. I believe, and the people of my constituency believe, that Kejimkujik park should be extended to include the Tobeatic game sanctuary area. I realize that part of the Tobeatic game site area is leased and is under active exploitation for pulp wood but that area could easily be left out. The rest of it should be included in the park so that the western part of the province does have the benefit of a national park.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
The present Kejimkujik park entrance is 150 miles away from the western end of Nova Scotia and under those conditions is not the magnet for tourists in western Nova Scotia it should be. Kejimkujik therefore does not serve as fully as it might as a tourist attraction. However, with the extension westward to include the Tobeatic area, it would serve that purpose. All that is necessary is to extend the existing roads from Shelburne, Yarmouth and Digby into the western end of the Tobeatic area. Kejimkujik at the present time, I believe, is considered of minimum size for a national park, but with the extension I recommend it would be of adequate proportions.
If western Nova Scotia does, as we hope it will, receive its share of secondary industry, then an adequate area for recreation would be desirable, quite aside from the attraction for tourists. 1 ask the minister to study with me a map that has been prepared by interested people from my constituency showing just

July 4, 1967
Supply-Indian Affairs how this could be done. I feel federal assistance could be given, as was done under the roads to resources program for the development of access roads to the area. I might add further that these roads could traverse the province connecting to the west end of the enlarged national park, and they would also serve for the transport of produce from the Atlantic shore to the bay of Fundy and to Digby.
According to an answer recently given in the house by the Minister of Transport, an adequate ferry service is soon to be developed from Digby to Saint John, thereby connecting that whole area of western Nova Scotia to the trans-Canada highway and the railroad systems into central Canada. There is another purpose that a road system I suggest would serve, and that is the development of access to an emergency airport for the Yarmouth international airport on the occasions fog prevents landings at Yarmouth.
This has to come or we will be subjected forever to a very second rate type of air service. I realize that some of these features pertain to other departments, but they are part of a package job. I ask the minister to consider this matter seriously. I shall be very willing to co-operate with him and to show him the maps to indicate how this proposal would benefit the constituency.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, without taking too much of the time of the committee, I do not want to miss the opportunity to draw to the minister's attention an area in my riding, Pointe-Bleue, with which the department is now concerned.
The minister is aware of the current projects in Pointe-Bleue. First of all, I wish to commend him and the government for their intention of handing over to the Indians within a few years the management of their own affairs. I hope that this transfer will be made systematically, but as fast as possible.
I also wish the minister all the co-operation possible from his officials in the completion of that task. We have been hearing about this event in Point-Bleue for some years, but I am afraid that the work is not always as efficient as the minister would like it to be, probably because we are lagging behind, in the reservations, as far as Indian competence is concerned. And I know what I am talking about, because I keep in close touch with those people. I have noticed that as soon as an Indian improves himself a little,-as soon as he gets some education and polish, it seems that a

strange power drives him outside his reservation to earn his living.
He is even offered a very interesting salary to do the same work. A young man, who might be a school teacher at Pointe-Bleue, is offered a higher salary to teach outside Pointe-Bleue, probably-and I am not saying that I am convinced of that, but it is a fact and I want to point it out to the minister-in order to get him away from the others, because he could become an enlightened and intelligent chief, able to lead his group.
I still trust the group of civil servants, most of whom are not Indians. I am still confident that they are sincere in their work, that they want to give a clear advantage to the Indians in order that they might apply for the jobs to which they are entitled. I have spoken about the matter in the house before and I went so far as to attack publicly an agent of the reservation. I shall not do so to-night, because he has been replaced. We now have a Mr. Gosselin who does an excellent job. 1 trust he is sincere and will put into practice the ideas the minister has expressed with regard to the reservations, namely, that, at long last, their management should be handed over to the Indians.
Conceivably, the officers of the Pointe Bleue reservation, 90 per cent of whom are white people, are highly interested in keeping their jobs, but certainly this is not in the interests of the Indians, who would be ready and capable to take over, so as to get into higher positions and, finally, in a few years, carry out government policies themselves.
I am sure that the minister is not aware of all those small transactions which do not often come to light, but which are very effective and always detrimental to the Indians.
I listened earlier to the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) who is much more familiar than I am with Indian affairs, and since I have been watching the activities of civil servants, I find that few are at fault, because most of them are doing a fine job, and I commend them for it. But even if there were only one or two, it would still be enough to delay the work of the department. That is why I call the minister's attention this evening to the things that we see. Let nobody think that we are keeping our eyes closed.
The minister announced the building of a sewage disposal and water distribution system in Pointe-Bleue at a cost of $1,500,000. I congratulate him but I regret that the project should be stretched over a period of five years. For 15 or 20 years at least, they have
July 4, 1967

been asking that the village streets of the Indian reservation be paved or that a few feet of sidewalk be built for there are no sidewalks and no paved streets in the reservation.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
As a result, the Indians will be in the midst of a construction upheaval for five years. During five years, the village will be upside down, precisely at the time when the provincial government will be paving the approaches to the reservation, as has been announced for the summer or at the beginning of the next year. For another five years, the village will be a ploughed field.
I have already suggested to the minister that a contractor would be interested in doing the work so as to pave the streets and build the sidewalks the same year. The same contractor is willing to wait five years for payment in accordance with the agreement, that is approximately $165,000 or $200,000 per year, according to the estimates of the department.
Well, I think that the minister should consider that proposal; the department would not find it too costly, the work could be done during the same year at the Indians' satisfaction.
The reservation is now made up of some 1,300 or 1,400 inhabitants. It is quite a big village and it seems to me that they have been living in the dust long enough to ask the federal government to do something for them. In all the small municipalities of 700, 800 or 900 inhabitants in my riding, streets are paved. But in Pointe Bleue, because that reservation comes under the federal government, nothing has been done.
The present project is of course better than nothing, but it would be ideal if the department considered the completion of their water and sewer systems during the same year, for they already have a housing project which is making good progress. Then, the possibility of paving the streets and building sidewalks could be considered.
Mr. Chairman, I do not want to speak longer; I just wanted to deal with that specific point, the amount to be spent in Pointe Bleue in the next few years. I am sure that if the minister looks squarely at the situation and if he takes into consideration the requests made by the band council of Pointe Bleue, he will do something.
I would have liked also to talk about the assistance that could be given to the Indians, especially in the field of private industry, in 27053-1421
Supply-Indian Affairs the reservations. I do not have much time tonight, because we must be through by ten o clock but, next fall, when we continue the study of those estimates, I will deal with the assistance as well as the protection that the government should give the Indians in the reservations.
Today, it is impossible for an Indian to go into business because he cannot get the necessary financing. As I said previously, the Hudson's Bay Company is still all powerful in the reservations. Unless the Indians are given an equal opportunity, there will be no point in transferring to them, some day, the administration of their own affairs. The private interests within the reservations must be respected in the first place.
Recommendations and reports are fine, but when you cannot implement them, it is useless to multiply investigations. You are bound to go around in circles and there is no escape.
There is a group of serious men in the Pointe-Bleue reservation who long for the day when they may at last do like all inhabitants of other municipalities, that is, set up their own businesses, and borrow money to operate their own affairs. I am convinced that if the minister makes an investigation-not through a royal commission but a private one directed by serious people-he will probably get to the heart of the matter and then he will be able to devise a policy, at least with respect to the Pointe-Bleue reservation.
If the Indian has lost confidence in the white man, who can blame him?
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
I should like to speak briefly in connection with our national parks. I am much afraid that in recent years the general policy with regard to the administration of the national parks has become sadly distorted as compared with what was undoubtedly the original purpose of parliament when the parks were set up. This purpose was to set aside certain areas in Canada so that the people would have full opportunity to enjoy them. Because of the difference in the types of parks there has been a considerable number of errors made as far as the administration of the parks is concerned.
The mountain parks with which I am particularly familiar, having been a resident of Alberta for 50 years during which period I have visited them frequently, are a totally different proposition from the much smaller parks in eastern Canada with which I have

July 4. 1967
Supply-Indian Affairs also become acquainted to some extent, particularly during the period when I was minister of this department, or its predecessor.
There has of course been a very strong lobby on the part of so-called conservationists to preserve the large western parks particularly as wilderness areas, and I have a great deal of sympathy with this point of view as long as it is not carried to excess. More recently there has been a great deal of difficulty in connection with the ownership of leases or leasing rights to land in the national parks. All this, along with the constant desire of the officials of any department to produce a tidy administration has obscured the basic purpose of our parks, which was to provide areas in which all the people of Canada should have the opportunity to relax and enjoy themselves and those parks.
In our mountain parks, unfortunately, this opportunity has never been provided, because in order to provide such an opportunity facilities must be made available, and this has never been done in the large parks in western Alberta and adjacent areas of British Columbia. Nothing like the amount of low-cost accommodation which would make it possible for the average Canadian to spend a few days in the parks with his family has been provided.
In order to cater for these visitors a considerable number of things have to be done. First it is necessary to provide camp sites. The parks administration has provided a considerable number of new camp sites during recent years and the situation has improved, but there are still nothing like as many camp sites as there should be to accommodate the large numbers of people who should be accommodated and who wish to be accommodated, to say nothing of those who will be visiting the parks in the future years.
Second, there has to be a greater provision of trailer camps. A large number of people who cannot afford to stay at a motel or in a hotel, paying between $10 and $20 a day, come in trailers, and there is still nothing like the number of trailer camp sites necessary to accommodate the people who presently wish to use them, to say nothing of the demand which will undoubtedly arise in the years immediately ahead.
Third, there must be a considerable increase in the number of low-cost motels and cabin camps. The first thing I attempted to change in the administration during the brief period I was minister in charge of national parks was the regulations laying down

specifications to be met before a trailer camp or motel could be put up. I am all in favour of having motels or cabin camps looking as attractive as possible, but you can have very attractive low-cost cabin camps or motels which blend in well with the natural surroundings of a park without the person who puts them up being required to spend a very large amount of money doing so.
This has been one of the great shortcomings of the parks throughout the entire 50 years I have been familiar with them. People have not been allowed to put up accommodation which they could rent during a comparatively short season at a price which an average low-income Canadian could afford to pay. It is no use having national parks which are available only to visitors with money or to Canadians with money. If these parks are to serve their purpose they must contain facilities which will enable our low-income group to spend some time in them. This has not been the case, it is not the case now, and it is one of the deficiencies which more than anything else needs to be corrected.
In addition, if people are to visit these parks and enjoy them you have to provide much better access by road than presently exists, and considerably more riding and walking trails. These are things in which the parks administration has in my view been deficient throughout the years. There has been on the part of a considerable number of people the idea that these large western parks should be preserved almost completely in their natural state and that it is a bad thing to put a road through, or a walking trail or a riding trail. But if this is not done, nobody can enjoy the parks, and the purpose for which the parks were set aside is defeated. It is in this respect that the general policy with regard to the parks has been wrong, in my submission, and must be corrected. Action becomes increasingly important as cities grow, as people are crowded together more and more and as there is greater necessity for them to get out into a wilderness, or semi-wilderness, area and enjoy their surroundings.
During the last two or three years the issue which has probably caused the minister the greatest amount of trouble has been that of leasing regulations. I would say that any leasing regulations which are to work from a practical point of view must give security of tenure to the person who has put up a building or bought it from somebody else. Under the present regulations a motel owner, for instance, has security of tenure for 21 years which is not sufficient to allow for the type of
July 4, 1967

development necessary if the people of Canada are to get into the parks and enjoy them.
At Lake Louise a motel site has been offered for tender three times, yet the department has received no bid because there is insufficient security of tenure to justify the investment of a large amount of capital. This will be the situation in all the parks unless we adopt leasing regulations which give sufficient security of tenure to encourage people to build accommodation essential to the enjoyment of the parks by our population. A great deal of the difficulty arises from the fact that there is a desire in any bureaucracy for a nice, tidy administration. I think the national parks branch should forget about a tidy administration and follow a policy which would enable the parks to be used by all the people of this country, rather than one which to a large extent excludes the majority of the people.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
I would have liked to say a few things about Indian affairs but I note it is ten minutes to ten o'clock, and one or two of my colleagues wish to make some remarks.

Mr. Chairman, I have very few observations to make in view of the time, but first I would like to say that I think the minister, since taking over this department, has been very encouraging to Indians in what he has done. Most hon. members have been pleased with the announcements he has made, particularly with regard to housing for Indians and other improvements. However, it is my experience that, despite his good intentions, and no doubt those of the senior officials of his department who may have suggested some of these things to him, many of his well-meaning plans have become sadly frustrated, due to the attitude of junior echelons in his department.
I have some knowledge of this, as I happened to be honorary chief of one band of Indians in Ontario, and visited them within the last two days. With respect to the question of housing there is something very interesting that should be brought to the minister's attention. A great deal of money has been put up by the government, with the approval of all hon. members, to provide Indians with better housing. It is the policy of the department that the Indians themselves do as much as they can themselves to help build their new houses. However, apparently the officials in the department seem to think bathrooms are not necessary for Indians.
This is strange to me because I am quite sure C.M.H.C. would not stand for houses being built without bathrooms in areas adjacent to large metropolitan centres. As most hon. members who have experience of dealing with C.M.H.C. know, it is almost impossible to get a loan from the corporation to build a house unless the plans include all kinds of sanitary provisions. But apparently this does not apply to Indians. As a result the inference many people get is that Indians are regarded by some departmental officials as some kind

July 4, 1967
Supp ly-Indian Affairs of second class citizens, and I would ask the minister to look into this matter.
Surely bathrooms are not a luxury in the southern part of Ontario and elsewhere, although they may well be in the far north permafrost area. Where Indian children are attending public schools and high schools which have these facilities, they should not be denied them at home.
The department has also done a lot to promote policies under which Indians on reserves are helped to carry on businesses for themselves. One example I have in mind is the building of a marina in the Georgian bay area. This is a good project. The Indians have hired an expert, who has run other marinas, to give them advice on the project. But the Indian agent comes prowling around every week and says, "This is wrong, that is wrong; this should be done, that should be done." I suspect he knows nothing about the work involved.
Further, tenders have to be invited for even the most trivial amounts of material. The manager that the Indians have employed says he could save money if he had authority to purchase material locally. Also in this regard, the department sends down large quantities of material that serve no useful purpose in the construction of the project. Only this afternoon I happened to see at this marina a large pile of stuff sent there by the department which is useless, and is just going to waste.
This brings me to another matter which I think should be considered by the appropriate parliamentary committee, namely the question of the usefulness of Indian agents in view of the government's new policies. I am not suggesting they should be gotten rid of at once, but if the Indian people are to achieve their own welfare this form of paternalism, particularly when it is exercised by people who are not always as competent as they might be, is unwise. I hope the minister will give consideration to the points I have raised.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the present government has done a good many mean and cruel things, but I suggest that nothing it has done is as mean or as cruel as what seems to be shaping up with regard to our retired civil servants. This issue of increasing the pensions of retired civil servants has been with us for a long long time; indeed in my experience-it has been with us for over 20 years. Finally in June of 1966 the present government consented to refer the matter of raising the pensions of retired civil servants to the special joint committee on the public service of Canada. That reference was actually made in January of 1967.
On May 8, 1967, that special joint committee made its report to both houses of parliament recommending that increases in the pensions of retired civil servants and also the pensions of retired armed forces and R.C.M.P. personnel be made. Since that time I have raised the matter in the House of Commons ten or a dozen times. Every time, until very recently at any rate, the answer has been to the effect that the matter was under active consideration. We were in fact led to believe before the committee made its report that if it made a unanimous recommendation, the government would act upon it. It is now more than eight weeks since that recommendation was made and yet here we are within a few days of taking a summer recess and it begins to look as though nothing is going to be done before parliament recesses for its summer break.
On May 8 the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Benson) assured me that the matter was under active consideration, the matter being the precise recommendation that increases be made. On May 15 the same Pres-sident of the Treasury Board told me the
July 4, 1967
2244	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion matter was presently under study. On May 25 the same President of the Treasury Board told me the government was making progress on the matter. On June 2 I put my question about this matter to the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson). I asked him whether it would be dealt with before a summer break. His answer was, "We will do our best". I thought that answer was worth something. I am beginning to think it was not worth the time it took him to say it. On June 12 I again put the question to the Prime Minister. He told me that the matter was under urgent consideration. I put it to him again on June 15 at which time he reminded me of his statement of three days earlier to the effect that the matter was under active and urgent consideration. As a supplementary question, I asked him why it could not be placed on the order paper within the next few days. I was brought to order at that time by the Chair and it was then that I decided to raise the question on an adjournment motion.
On June 22 I again asked whether there would be any action on this matter before the house rises for a summer break and again I was told by the President of the Treasury Board that the matter was under active consideration. On June 26, in the absence of the Prime Minister and the President of the Treasury Board, I put the question to the government house leader, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Mac-Eachen), who assured me that he would bring the matter to the attention of the Prime Minister and the President of the Treasury Board.
On June 30, last Friday, I asked the President of the Treasury Board whether, in view of the attention that has been given to this matter, he could get the legislation for increases in civil service pensions on the order paper so we could deal with it this week, before parliament recesses for a summer break. His reply was that he did not think this was possible although the matter was receiving the consideration of the government. That means, unless I do not understand the plain meaning of words, that the government has no intention of acting on this matter before this house rises for the summer recess.
On the last two or three occasions when I asked this question I have been greeted with impatient murmurs from the other side of the house. The only audible words I could get were: Why don't you wait; this is going to be done? To say to old retired servants of the federal government who have been waiting for months and years for this increase that


they should wait still longer, that they should wait until the fall, is the ultimate in cruelty.
I am sure that between now and the fall other matters will arise which will be given higher priority and it will be October or November before we get to this legislation; and it will be December or January before any increases are added to the cheques of these retired civil servants. Many of these people will not need the increases because they will have died before the increases come through. If, as I believe, the government has made up its mind that it is going to go along with the recommendations of the special joint committee on the public service of Canada, and if, as I believe, the government is going to act on this matter in the fall, why not do so now? What rhyme or reason is there to putting off any longer the action that must be taken on this issue?
In my view this House of Commons should not break for a summer recess until it has dealt with this matter. I feel very strongly about this. We have a house order that requires certain business to be completed by Thursday night of this week, and no individual member can stop that, but there is still the question as to whether we are going to rise on Friday for a recess of a period of time not yet stated, and I for one feel we should not do that. I for one will not agree to our rising on Friday unless the government gives us the satisfaction of answering this important question.
To my knowledge these people have been put off for 20 to 25 years, those who have been around that long. The government has been dilly-dallying and boondoggling with this issue for many months, since it came to power, and for weeks since the committee made its report. I insist that the time for action is now, and by "now" I mean before this house rises for a summer break.

Mr. Speaker, I must first of all thank the parliamentary secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Macdonald), for having willingly added a few additional minutes to his arduous day in order to answer my question.
A few years ago, the Canadian government decided to open a consulate in Louisiana, more specifically in New Orleans. Since then, it has been found that the consulate has fallen far short of expectations at the time of its establishment. It is not that the representation over there is deficient, that the choice was untimely, but rather that the activities that had been expected did not materialize.
And these consulates, scattered here and there, more often serve as commercial posts rather than centres of diplomatic activity.
That is precisely the case with the consulate at New Orleans which, with that in Los Angeles, serves the southern states. That consulate, when all commercial activities are finally added up, gives far from impressive results.
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
Therefore, that is my first reason for proposing that the consulate should be closed and replaced by another one that could perhaps be located in the state of Florida.
The second reason in favour of such a consulate in the state of Florida is precisely that thousands of our nationals are found in Florida throughout the year, whether as tourists or as people who, after several years of hard work, choose to retire there. Consequently, the presence of those thousands of Canadian nationals is more than enough to warrant the establishment of a place for reference, of a consulate in Florida, a much more appropriate location than Louisiana.
The third reason I would like to give is the following: the state of Florida is much more important, on the basis of population and on the basis of area, than the state of Louisiana.
The fourth reason is that the state of Florida is more industrialized and the space research centre which is located there represents a growth factor for all kinds of activities, the scope of which is difficult to anticipate.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, the last reason I would like to submit is that the establishment of the consulate in Florida would, first of all, permit the establishment of a relationship between the Caribbean and Canada and then with the other southern states on the Atlantic coast which are an uncommon tourist attraction for thousands of Canadian citizens.
For all those reasons, I believe that it would be appropriate to repeat the suggestion I made at the beginning, that is to close the consulate in Louisiana, because it is not useful enough, and to open a consulate in Florida either at Tallahassee, Tampa or Miami, to give better service to the Canadian people who regularly visit the state of Florida.

On this memorable milestone in our history-made more memorable and joyful by your gracious presence-after a century of sun and storm, we beg to tell Your Majesty that our devotion to the Crown has grown in depth and strength, and to speak humbly of our affection for your person.
